problems.title: Kelvin's problem in epithelia
problems.question: What is the energy-minimizing partition of space into equal-volume cells (Kelvin's problem, still open), and do cells in curved epithelia adopt the minimal shapes (scutoids) that the corresponding constrained problem predicts?
problems.known_state: Kelvin's 1887 conjecture was beaten by the Weaire-Phelan foam (1994); no proof of optimality for any 3D partition exists, in contrast to Hales's proof of the 2D honeycomb conjecture (2001). Gomez-Galvez et al. (2018) showed that cells in curved epithelia adopt scutoid shapes and argued they minimize energy; Thompson's cell-packing claims (ch07) are the 2D and 3D precursors and the repo's cell-geometry project segments micrographs for them.
acceptance_criteria: For the biological part: a pre-registered test on segmented 3D epithelial datasets comparing observed scutoid frequency against energy-minimizing predictions for the measured curvature, with a stated tolerance.

For the mathematical part: a new rigorous result, for example a Lean-checked lower bound on the surface area of equal-volume partitions in a periodic cell, or a computer-assisted proof of local optimality for Weaire-Phelan.
falsifiers: A partition with lower surface area than Weaire-Phelan would overturn the biological energy-minimization comparison baseline; scutoid frequencies far from the minimal-energy prediction would refute the energy-minimization account.
problems.data_access: Gomez-Galvez 2018 supplementary data (open); EM epithelial volumes (open repositories).

approaches.title: Computer-assisted proof that Weaire–Phelan is a strict local minimum among periodic foams
approaches.method: Prove local optimality of the Weaire–Phelan (WP) partition within its periodic class, the result the problem asks for. Setting: partitions of the 3-torus ℝ³/Λ (the WP cubic cell, 8 cells) into cells of equal volume. WP's faces are constant-mean-curvature surfaces meeting at Plateau angles. Plan: (a) compute the WP equilibrium with Surface Evolver at high refinement with an a-posteriori error bound; (b) compute the second variation (the Jacobi operator on faces with the Plateau-border coupling conditions and volume constraints) discretized by finite elements; (c) certify, with interval arithmetic in Arb, a lower bound λ_min > 0 on the constrained Hessian's smallest non-trivial eigenvalue, modulo translations, using a residual-based enclosure (Kato–Temple or Lehmann–Goerisch bounds) that converts discrete eigenvalue estimates into rigorous bounds for the continuous operator. A positive bound proves WP is a strict local minimum against all smooth volume-preserving perturbations periodic on Λ. The same pipeline applied to Kelvin's foam reproduces known stability as a validation.
steps: Compute WP and Kelvin equilibria in Surface Evolver; validate surface areas against published values (Kelvin 5.306, WP 5.288 in units of V^(2/3) for total cell surface).
Discretize the constrained second variation; compute the lowest eigenvalues numerically.
Derive rigorous eigenvalue lower bounds with Lehmann–Goerisch and Arb interval arithmetic.
Validate on Kelvin; publish the certificate and code.
approaches.decisive_result: A certified bound λ_min > 0 for WP's constrained second variation on its periodic cell, proving strict local optimality among equal-volume partitions with that period, the first rigorous optimality-type statement for WP.
approaches.failure_signature: The discrete-to-continuous error bound for curved faces with Plateau-border junctions cannot be made rigorous with available eigenvalue-enclosure methods, or the certified margin is negative within error, leaving the result unproved.
approaches.missing: Rigorous spectral enclosure for operators on foam networks with singular junction lines is research-level numerical analysis.

approaches.title: Lean-checked lower bounds on equal-volume partition area
approaches.method: Prove a rigorous lower bound in Lean for surface area per cell of any partition of a 3-torus into N equal-volume cells, and state its distance from WP. Bound 1 (isoperimetric half-sphere): each cell has surface ≥ (36π)^{1/3} V^{2/3}, every interior face is shared by two cells, so partition area per cell ≥ ½(36π)^{1/3}V^{2/3} ≈ 2.418, against WP's ≈ 2.644 (half of 5.288), a gap of about 9%. This requires the 3D isoperimetric inequality, which as far as we know is not in Mathlib. Formalize it via the Brunn–Minkowski inequality for compact sets (Mathlib's measure theory supports a Prékopa–Leindler route) and the Minkowski-content definition of surface area, or state it as an explicit hypothesis in a first version. Bound 2: tighten using Kusner's face-count argument, that cells in a minimal foam have a bounded average number of faces, combined with a lower bound on the area of a polyhedral-like cell with k faces of constant curvature, giving a bound above 2.418.
steps: Survey Mathlib for Brunn–Minkowski or Prékopa–Leindler; formalize the missing piece or state the isoperimetric inequality as a hypothesis in version 1.
Prove Bound 1 for partitions of the 3-torus (shared-face accounting as a finite-sum lemma).
Formalize the face-count argument and the per-cell bound for Bound 2, if Bound 1 completes.
Report the numerical gap to WP and Kelvin.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean theorem bounding area per cell of any equal-volume 3-torus partition from below, unconditional if the isoperimetric inequality is formalized, otherwise conditional on it as a named hypothesis, with the gap to WP stated. Bound 2 above 2.418 would be new.
approaches.failure_signature: The isoperimetric inequality proves too large to formalize in a month, leaving only the conditional version, which is correct but adds little beyond the statement on paper.
approaches.missing: Geometric measure theory in Mathlib is thin; an unconditional isoperimetric inequality in ℝ³ is a substantial formalization project.

approaches.title: Scutoid frequency vs curvature in segmented 3D epithelia against minimal energy
approaches.method: Biological part. For each 3D epithelial dataset (Gómez-Gálvez et al. 2018 salivary glands and egg chambers; PlantSeg Arabidopsis ovule and lateral-root volumes as a curved plant epithelium; other open segmented volumes on IDR and EMPIAR), compute per-cell apico-basal neighbour exchanges (scutoid indicator) and the local radial expansion ratio s = R_basal/R_apical from fitted tissue surfaces. Prediction: run a 3D Voronoi tube model (Gómez-Gálvez 2018) and a Surface Evolver relaxed-foam model on a tube or ellipsoid with the measured s, cell number and cell-size dispersion, giving the predicted scutoid fraction p̂(s) with simulation intervals. Pre-registered tolerance: supports energy minimization if observed scutoid fractions fall within the 95% simulation band at ≥ 80% of curvature bins pooled across datasets; refutes if observed fractions are outside the band in the same direction in ≥ 50% of bins. Also test the Gómez-Gálvez et al. 2022 biophysical principle linking connectivity to s.
steps: Pre-register datasets' admission criteria (3D cell segmentation with apical and basal surfaces), binning of s and the tolerance.
Download and checksum datasets; compute scutoid indicators and s per cell.
Run the Voronoi and relaxed-foam simulations at measured parameters; build p̂(s) bands.
Compare and report the verdict per dataset and pooled.
approaches.decisive_result: Observed versus predicted scutoid fraction across curvature bins in at least three independent tissue types, with a pre-registered verdict on whether cells adopt minimal-energy packings for their curvature.
approaches.failure_signature: Segmentation errors in apical or basal surfaces create spurious neighbour exchanges at rates comparable to predicted scutoid fractions (estimate the error rate on manually checked cells); then the test is measurement-limited.

approaches.title: Curvature-blinded scutoid frequency test
approaches.method: Segment at least 30 epithelial volumes spanning curvature and thickness, with at least 200 cells each. Before inspecting topology, predict scutoid frequency from a vertex-model energy minimized at measured curvature, cell-number mismatch and apicobasal tension ratio. Test predictions on held-out tissues and compare to topology-preserving random rearrangements.
steps: Validate segmentation topology against manually annotated cells with F1 above 0.95.
Freeze energy parameters using flat epithelia only.
Predict per-volume scutoid fraction and spatial localization.
Compare absolute error and likelihood to random and curvature-only baselines.
approaches.decisive_result: Energy minimization is supported if held-tissue scutoid-frequency error is below 0.1 and at least 50% lower than both baselines, with correct localization in 80% of volumes.
approaches.failure_signature: Predicted frequency is systematically wrong by more than 0.2 or segmentation uncertainty changes scutoid calls by over 10%.
approaches.missing: Enough open volumetric epithelia with diverse measured curvatures.

approaches.title: Certified local optimality of Weaire-Phelan
approaches.method: Restrict the mathematical problem to periodic partitions with fixed Weaire-Phelan combinatorics and finite-dimensional face perturbations. Compute the second variation of area under volume constraints, quotient translation and gauge modes, and certify positive definiteness with interval arithmetic; formalize the constrained Hessian argument in Lean.
steps: Specify a finite periodic fundamental cell and exact constraint manifold.
Derive first- and second-variation formulas symbolically.
Bound geometric coefficients and Hessian eigenvalues by intervals.
Check a Lean theorem converting the certificate to strict local minimality in the restricted class.
approaches.decisive_result: A checked positive lower bound on the constrained Hessian after all symmetry zero modes are removed, proving strict local optimality for the declared perturbation class.
approaches.failure_signature: A certified negative mode gives an explicit area-lowering perturbation, disproving local optimality in that class.
approaches.missing: A tractable exact representation of curved interfaces and a bridge from finite perturbations to arbitrary variations.

approaches.title: Scutoid frequency against curvature in the 2018 data
approaches.method: Use the supplementary tables of Gómez-Gálvez et al. 2018, not a re-segmentation, unless the tables lack per-tissue scutoid frequencies. If they lack frequencies, stop as data-unavailable rather than tracing figures. The prediction is the paper's own energy-minimizing scutoid fraction as a function of the measured curvature and cell aspect ratio. Pre-register success as either every curvature bin within 10 percentage points of the predicted fraction, or a Spearman correlation above 0.8 between predicted and observed fractions across bins. Bins are the paper's bins. A new segmentation pipeline is a different project and is not a rescue if the tables are insufficient.
steps: Read the supplement and stop if frequencies and curvatures are not numeric.
Transcribe bin-wise scutoid fractions and curvatures with a checksum.
Compute the paper's predicted fraction at each bin.
Apply the 10-point tolerance and the Spearman threshold.
Support the energy account only if one of the two pre-registered conditions holds.
approaches.decisive_result: Either all bins within 10 percentage points of the predicted scutoid fraction, or Spearman correlation above 0.8.
approaches.failure_signature: Both conditions fail. The energy-minimizing scutoid prediction then does not fit the paper's own binned data. Missing numeric tables are inconclusive, not a refutation.
approaches.missing: If the supplement contains images rather than frequencies, the swarm lacks the numeric table and should not invent one by tracing.

approaches.title: Anneal equal-volume foams against Weaire–Phelan
approaches.method: Use Brakke's Surface Evolver. First reproduce the surface area per unit volume of Kelvin's truncated octahedron and of the Weaire–Phelan foam in the same normalization, to a relative tolerance of 10^{-4}. Then anneal 200 random equal-volume periodic foams with 8 cells and 200 with 16 cells, from random seeds declared in advance, with a fixed iteration budget. A counterexample is a foam whose area per unit volume is lower than the reproduced Weaire–Phelan value by more than 10^{-4}. Failure to find one does not prove optimality. The approach settles the mathematical problem only in the counterexample direction. Reproducing the two known areas is a check, not a solution of Kelvin's problem.
steps: Reproduce Kelvin and Weaire–Phelan areas to relative 10^{-4}.
Declare seeds and the iteration budget.
Anneal 200 eight-cell foams and 200 sixteen-cell foams.
Compare the best area with Weaire–Phelan.
Publish the best foam if it wins, otherwise the negative search record.
approaches.decisive_result: A periodic equal-volume foam whose Surface Evolver area is more than 10^{-4} below the reproduced Weaire–Phelan area, or an honest negative record of the 400-foam search.
approaches.failure_signature: The search returns Weaire–Phelan as the best candidate. Kelvin's problem stays open. A failure of reproduction beyond 10^{-4} invalidates the comparison.
approaches.missing: A certificate of global optimality. Annealing cannot supply one. Thirty years of search have not beaten Weaire–Phelan, so a month of random starts is unlikely to.

approaches.title: Lean-check a lower bound and the Kelvin–Weaire gap
approaches.method: Two checked statements, neither of which is global optimality. First, formalize a lower bound on surface area for a periodic partition into equal-volume cells that is strictly stronger than the single-cell isoperimetric inequality obtained by ignoring shared faces, and prove it in Lean with interval arithmetic where a radical is involved. Second, formalize the areas of the Kelvin truncated octahedron and the Weaire–Phelan cell in the same normalization and prove the Weaire–Phelan area is smaller, to a stated interval. The acceptance criteria allow a Lean-checked lower bound that does not identify the minimizer. Do not describe the comparison of two candidates as a lower bound on all partitions.
steps: Prove a shared-face lower bound above the isolated-sphere area.
Compute Kelvin's cell area as an interval.
Compute the Weaire–Phelan area as an interval.
Prove the Weaire–Phelan interval lies strictly below Kelvin's.
State that global optimality remains open, and audit axioms.
approaches.decisive_result: A no-sorry lower bound strictly above the isolated-sphere area, and a no-sorry inequality that the Weaire–Phelan cell has smaller area than Kelvin's cell.
approaches.failure_signature: The bound does not exceed the isolated-sphere area, or the interval arithmetic cannot separate the two foam areas. The approach has then not produced the promised checked comparison.
approaches.missing: A proof of optimality for any three-dimensional partition. This approach does not claim one.

problems.title: Predict which genes show mutant-morphant discrepancies
problems.question: Can a rule be learned and validated that predicts, from a gene's sequence, paralog structure and network position, whether its zebrafish CRISPR mutant will lack the phenotype its morpholino knockdown shows (transcriptional adaptation / genetic compensation)?
problems.known_state: Kok et al. (2015) found most morphant phenotypes absent in mutants; Rossi et al. (2015) showed genetic compensation; El-Brolosy et al. (2019) identified the mechanism as transcriptional adaptation triggered by mutant mRNA decay and upregulating sequence-similar genes. Which genes compensate is not predictable in advance. Already a Frontier Problem.
acceptance_criteria: A pre-registered classifier using ZFIN mutant and morphant phenotype records as labels and INDRA CoGEx paralog, NMD-pathway and network features as predictors, with held-out accuracy and the chance baseline stated in advance.
A ranked list of untested genes with predicted compensation, so the prediction can be checked by future experiments.
falsifiers: Held-out accuracy at the baseline refutes the predictability claim with present features.
problems.data_access: ZFIN (open), INDRA CoGEx (public MCP), Ensembl paralog tables (open).

related_claims.label: Cave animals are related to surface fauna of their own continent
Genes for morphogenesis and for learning and memory should overlap widely

approaches.title: Pre-registered classifier from ZFIN labels with paralog, NMD and network features
approaches.method: Labels: from ZFIN downloads, genes with at least one morpholino phenotype and at least one phenotyped mutant allele. A gene is 'discrepant' if the mutant lacks the morphant's phenotype in the same anatomical system and stage window, and 'concordant' otherwise; this rule is fixed in advance and applied by script. Features, fixed in advance: (a) paralog structure (number of zebrafish paralogs including ohnologs from Ensembl Compara, maximum protein identity, and whether the closest paralog is co-expressed in the same tissue per ZFIN expression); (b) NMD susceptibility of the mutant allele (premature termination codon more than 50 nt upstream of the last exon junction, from allele annotation); (c) network features from INDRA CoGEx on human orthologs (degree, number of upstream regulators, membership in complexes); (d) gene length and expression level. Models: L1-regularized logistic regression and gradient-boosted trees, nested cross-validation, with a gene-family-grouped split so paralogs never span train and test. Pre-registered: success if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.70 against a feature-free baseline of 0.5 (permutation p < 0.01). Output: a ranked list of untested genes by predicted discrepancy probability.
steps: Write result.json with label rule, features, model, split and threshold before computing labels.
Download ZFIN phenotype, morpholino and allele files; Ensembl paralog tables; query CoGEx; record versions and checksums.
Construct labels and features; run nested grouped cross-validation.
Report AUROC with CI, feature importances and the ranked prediction list for genes lacking mutant data.
approaches.decisive_result: Held-out AUROC with 95% CI under gene-family-grouped cross-validation against the 0.5 baseline, plus a published ranked list of predictions for genes whose mutants are not yet phenotyped, so future ZFIN records check the prediction.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than about 150 genes have both morphant and mutant phenotypes comparable in system and stage, or AUROC CI includes 0.5: refutes predictability with present features.

approaches.title: Two-feature transcriptional-adaptation rule tested as a single hypothesis
approaches.method: Instead of a flexible classifier, test the mechanism's own prediction as one pre-registered hypothesis with no tuning. From El-Brolosy et al. 2019 and Ma et al. 2019, transcriptional adaptation requires mutant mRNA decay (an NMD-triggering PTC allele) and upregulates genes sharing sequence similarity with the mutated gene. Rule: predict 'discrepant' iff (i) the phenotyped mutant allele is PTC-bearing and NMD-sensitive and (ii) a paralog with ≥ 50% nucleotide identity over the region of similarity exists. Predict 'concordant' otherwise, including promoter-less or whole-gene deletion alleles, which the mechanism predicts do not compensate. Compute the 2 × 2 contingency table against ZFIN-derived labels (same rule as approach 1), Fisher's exact test, and the odds ratio. Pre-registered: supports if OR ≥ 3 with a 95% CI lower bound > 1.5. A natural experiment within the data: genes with both a PTC allele and a promoter-less allele phenotyped, where the mechanism predicts discordance only for the PTC allele.
steps: Pre-register the two-feature rule, identity threshold and statistics.
Annotate allele classes from ZFIN (PTC position relative to last exon junction; deletion type).
Compute paralog identities (Ensembl Compara plus nucleotide alignment of the similarity region).
Run Fisher's test; analyse the within-gene PTC versus promoter-less contrast separately.
approaches.decisive_result: Odds ratio for discrepancy given the two-feature mechanistic signature, and within-gene allele contrasts. A strong association, especially in within-gene contrasts, would turn transcriptional adaptation into a quantitative predictor; OR ≈ 1 would show it does not explain most discrepancies.
approaches.failure_signature: Too few genes have promoter-less or whole-gene-deletion alleles phenotyped (fewer than 15) for the within-gene contrast; and allele PTC annotation is missing for many ZFIN alleles.

approaches.title: Confound audit: do morpholino properties, not gene properties, predict it?
approaches.method: A rival explanation of mutant–morphant discrepancy is morpholino artefact: off-target binding and p53-mediated toxicity give phenotypes the true loss of function would not. If so, discrepancy should be predicted by properties of the morpholino, not the gene. For each morpholino in ZFIN with a target and phenotype, compute: (a) the number of off-target sites in the zebrafish transcriptome with ≤ 2 mismatches (translation-start and splice-site windows, by alignment against Ensembl transcripts); (b) whether reported phenotypes include the nonspecific toxicity signature (necrosis, pericardial oedema, small head and eyes) in the same annotations; (c) morpholino type (translation-blocking or splice-blocking) and whether rescue or p53 co-knockdown is annotated. Fit a logistic model of discrepancy on morpholino features alone, gene features alone (approach 1's), and both, with nested grouped cross-validation. Pre-registered: the artefact explanation dominates if morpholino features alone reach AUROC within 0.03 of the combined model and gene features add < 0.03.
steps: Pre-register the toxicity signature terms, off-target search parameters and comparison thresholds.
Extract morpholino sequences and targets from ZFIN; run the off-target alignment.
Fit morpholino-only, gene-only and combined models with the same splits as approach 1.
Report AUROCs and the incremental contribution of each feature group.
approaches.decisive_result: The relative predictive contribution of morpholino properties versus gene properties to mutant–morphant discrepancy. Dominance of morpholino features attributes most discrepancies to artefact; dominance of gene features supports compensation, the Frontier problem's attribution question.
approaches.failure_signature: Morpholino and gene features are confounded (genes with paralogs are also targeted by morpholinos with more off-target sites), so the incremental AUROCs cannot be separated; report the overlap instead of a verdict.

approaches.title: Leakage-proof ZFIN discrepancy classifier
approaches.method: Construct gene-level labels only where mutant and morpholino experiments test matched developmental stages and phenotypes. Predict discrepancy using paralog sequence similarity, NMD susceptibility, duplicate age, baseline expression, INDRA network redundancy and annotation counts. Hold out entire paralog families and publication years to prevent near-gene and literature leakage.
steps: Double-label records and require adjudicated agreement above kappa 0.8.
Freeze positive, negative and uncertain definitions before feature extraction.
Require at least 100 positives and 100 matched negatives.
Compare calibrated gradient boosting with logistic and prevalence baselines in nested group cross-validation.
approaches.decisive_result: Predictability requires family-held-out AUROC at least 0.75, AUPRC at least twice prevalence and calibration slope between 0.8 and 1.2; bootstrap lower bounds must exceed baselines.
approaches.failure_signature: Performance collapses below AUROC 0.6 under family or temporal holdout, showing apparent prediction was leakage or annotation bias.
approaches.missing: A clean matched ZFIN label set; phenotype ontology mappings and negative labels require manual curation.

approaches.title: Mechanistic compensation score from decay and paralogs
approaches.method: Build an interpretable score from predicted premature termination and NMD, mutant-transcript abundance, sequence similarity to expressed paralogs, and signed compensatory paths in INDRA. Evaluate the prespecified score without learned weights, then use causal mediation on datasets containing mutant RNA-seq to test whether paralog upregulation mediates phenotype absence.
steps: Define the score and thresholds before joining phenotype labels.
Select at least 50 mutants with RNA-seq, matched knockdown phenotype and paralog information.
Test score discrimination and paralog-expression mediation with bootstrap uncertainty.
Rank untested genes only after the held-out threshold is met.
approaches.decisive_result: Mechanistic support requires odds ratio at least 2 per score SD, AUROC above 0.7 and a positive mediated fraction above 0.3 with 95% interval excluding zero.
approaches.failure_signature: NMD and paralog induction do not precede phenotype rescue, mediation is null, or discrimination is at chance.
approaches.missing: Public mutant RNA-seq paired to rigorously matched morphant and mutant phenotypes.

approaches.title: Test the NMD-plus-paralog rule on all doubly assayed genes
approaches.method: Labels come from ZFIN downloads: Morpholinos.txt, CRISPR.txt, and phenoGeneCleanData_fish.txt. A gene is labeled only if it has both a morpholino phenotype and at least one mutant or CRISPR allele. It is a discrepancy if the morpholino is abnormal for an anatomy term and no mutant or CRISPR allele of that gene is abnormal for that term. Genes with no mutant are unlabeled, not counted as concordant. The rule, frozen first: predict discrepancy if and only if a representative frameshift or nonsense lesion lies more than 50 nucleotides upstream of the last exon-exon junction, the vertebrate nonsense-mediated-decay position rule, and Ensembl reports a paralogue with at least 70 percent identity over at least half the length. Hold out entire paralogue families, not single genes. The rule supports predictability if, on the held-out families, precision is at least 0.6 and the bootstrap interval for precision minus the base rate excludes 0. Report recall and do not require it to match precision.
steps: Build labels from the three ZFIN files with the anatomy-term rule.
Annotate NMD position and Ensembl paralogue identity.
Hold out paralogue families.
Apply the Boolean rule.
Require held-out precision at least 0.6 and a bootstrap interval for precision minus base rate that excludes 0.
approaches.decisive_result: Held-out precision at least 0.6 with a bootstrap interval for precision minus the discrepancy base rate excluding 0.
approaches.failure_signature: The interval for precision minus base rate contains 0. The rule then does not beat the base rate, which refutes predictability of this form.
approaches.missing: The 50-nucleotide rule is the mammalian exon-junction convention. Zebrafish may differ, and a failure may mean the threshold is wrong rather than that compensation is unpredictable.

approaches.title: Family-held-out logistic model with an INDRA ablation
approaches.method: Same labels and the same paralogue-family holdout. Fit an L2-regularized logistic regression. Feature block S: the NMD indicator, maximum paralogue identity, and paralogue count from Ensembl. Feature block I: INDRA degree and the presence of an INDRA edge to a paralogue. The full model uses both. Predictability is an area under the ROC curve above 0.70 on held-out families. The sequence block is the carrier if it beats the INDRA-only model by a DeLong test at p below 0.01 and the INDRA-only model does not itself clear 0.70. Nested cross-validation inside the training families chooses the L2 penalty. Do not use a random gene split, which leaks paralogues.
steps: Reuse the ZFIN labels and the family partition.
Build sequence features and INDRA features.
Choose the L2 penalty inside training families only.
Score held-out AUROC for the full model, block S and block I.
DeLong-test block S against block I.
approaches.decisive_result: Held-out AUROC above 0.70 for the sequence block, and a DeLong p-value below 0.01 against the INDRA-only block if that comparison is needed to assign the signal.
approaches.failure_signature: Held-out AUROC at or below 0.70 for every block. Present features then do not predict discrepancy. An AUROC that collapses when families are held out after looking strong on a random split is leakage, not a result.

approaches.title: Score untested morpholino genes and check calibration
approaches.method: The acceptance criteria ask for a ranked list of genes not yet tested as mutants. Fit the one-parameter mechanistic score P(discrepancy) = logistic(a + b times maximum paralogue identity + c times the NMD indicator) on the training families from the Boolean-rule split. The score must beat an intercept-only model on held-out families by a likelihood-ratio test at p below 0.01, and the reliability diagram of deciles must be monotone. Only then score genes that have a morpholino phenotype and no mutant allele. Publish the top 50 with the three features and the score. The list is a prediction, not a confirmation. Future experiments are outside the approach. A non-monotone reliability diagram fails the list even if the likelihood-ratio test passes.
steps: Fit a, b and c on training families only.
Likelihood-ratio test against the intercept on held-out families.
Build the decile reliability diagram and require monotonicity.
Score morpholino genes that have no mutant allele.
Publish the top 50 with features and scores.
approaches.decisive_result: A likelihood-ratio p-value below 0.01 against the intercept, a monotone decile reliability diagram, and a published top-50 list of untested genes.
approaches.failure_signature: The likelihood-ratio test misses 0.01, or the reliability diagram is not monotone. No list is published in those cases.
approaches.missing: Laboratory tests of the top 50. The swarm can publish the list and cannot confirm it.

problems.title: Do trabeculae align with principal stress, and is that alignment causal?
problems.question: In loaded cancellous bone (femoral head, vertebral body, calcaneus), is the mean trabecular orientation within a small angular tolerance of the principal stress directions computed from the bone's own geometry and a physiological load case? Is the alignment stronger than expected from a load-independent growth rule, and does it re-orient after experimentally altered loading?
problems.known_state: Wolff (1892) and Thompson (1917, ch. 16) hold that trabeculae lie along trajectories of principal stress because material off those lines is shear-loaded and remodelled away. Finite-element and remodelling models reproduce aligned architectures (Huiskes et al. 2000), and in vivo load-orientation experiments in bird and sheep joints report re-orientation (Pontzer et al. 2006; Barak et al. 2011), but results are mixed on how tight the alignment is, on whether alignment reflects the loads of habitual or peak activity, and on whether a purely genetic or developmental pattern would give the same fabric. Christen et al. 2014 find human remodelling load-driven but not lazy. No standardized, pre-registered cross-site and cross-species estimate of the stress-fabric angle with a developmental null exists.
acceptance_criteria: A pre-registered test on at least three open micro-CT datasets of loaded bone sites from at least two species: compute the mean-intercept-length fabric tensor, compute principal stresses from a stated finite-element load case, report the angular error distribution, and compare it against a null with the same density field but randomized fabric directions and against a growth-rule null. State the angular tolerance and the pass threshold in advance.
falsifiers: A median fabric-to-stress angular error not distinguishable from the randomized-fabric null, or insensitive to the choice of load case, would refute stress alignment as the dominant organizing principle at the tested sites.
Reproducible failure to re-orient after a documented change in joint loading would refute the causal claim.
problems.data_access: Open micro-CT of femora, vertebrae and calcanei on MorphoSource, Dryad and Zenodo; paired load data are the main uncertainty and have to be established by scouting before the test is pre-registered.

related_claims.label: Trabeculae of cancellous bone follow the lines of compressive and tensile stress
Shear removes obliquely laid trabeculae, leaving those aligned with stress lines
Trabecular architecture remodels to new force patterns after malunited fracture
Skeletal form is largely a diagram of mechanical stress

approaches.title: Pre-registered fabric-versus-principal-stress angle on open femoral micro-CT
approaches.method: On open micro-CT of loaded cancellous bone, compute the local fabric tensor (mean intercept length, via BoneJ anisotropy) in a grid of cubic volumes of interest (edge about 5 mm in human femoral heads, scaled to trabecular spacing in other species) and the local principal stress tensor from a homogenized finite-element model of the same bone under a stated physiological load case (hip contact force direction and magnitude from Bergmann et al. 2001 / OrthoLoad for human femur). The statistic is, per volume, the angle between the primary fabric eigenvector and the principal stress direction of largest absolute magnitude, folded to 0-90 degrees. Two nulls are fixed in advance: (a) randomized fabric with the same density field, for which an isotropic random axis has median angle 60 degrees (P(angle <= theta) = 1 - cos theta); (b) a load-independent growth-rule null in which fabric follows a geometric field of the bone alone (local direction of the shaft or neck axis, and the gradient of distance to the cortical shell). Load-case sensitivity is tested by sweeping the load direction over a cone of 60 degrees around the physiological direction and recording the direction that minimizes median angular error; alignment is credited to load only if the best direction lies inside the physiological range and the error rises away from it.
steps: Scout and register datasets: human proximal femora (Twente/VPHOP femur database, FEMHALS if a data-use agreement can be signed, the CC BY Figshare femur section), plus at least one non-human loaded site on MorphoSource (primate or ungulate femoral head, calcaneus or vertebra) with licence recorded.

Pre-register in test-data/claim-tests/thompson-growth-form/thompson1917-ch16-05/: VOI size, fabric method, FE material law (density-dependent isotropic modulus, so fabric does not enter the stress computation), load case, angular tolerance (median error <= 20 degrees), and the pass rule (median error below both nulls at p < 0.01 by permutation, in at least three sites from two species).
Segment with a fixed global threshold (Otsu per scan, recorded), compute MIL fabric per VOI with BoneJ, discard VOIs with degree of anisotropy below 1.1 where the primary axis is undefined.
Build voxel or tetrahedral homogenized FE meshes (FEniCSx), apply the load case, extract principal stresses per VOI.
Compute angular error distributions, the two nulls (1,000 permutations for the randomized null), and the load-direction sweep; report all three sites separately and pooled.

Stratify by local stress anisotropy (sigma1 - sigma3)/(|sigma1| + |sigma3|): the stress-alignment hypothesis predicts error falls as anisotropy rises; the growth-rule null predicts no such dependence.
approaches.decisive_result: Median fabric-to-stress angle at or below 20 degrees in at least three sites from two species, significantly below both the randomized-fabric null (median 60 degrees) and the geometric growth-rule null, with the best-fitting load direction inside the physiological cone and error decreasing with stress anisotropy.
approaches.failure_signature: Median angle not distinguishable from the growth-rule null, or the error minimum in the load sweep lying outside the physiological cone or being flat (load-case insensitive); or fewer than three usable loaded sites with licences after scouting, in which case the approach stalls rather than refutes.
approaches.missing: Licensed non-human micro-CT of loaded sites with known habitual loads; FEMHALS raw scans need an operator-signed data-use agreement; homogenized FE of whole bones is computationally heavy but feasible.

approaches.title: Calibrate the growth-rule null and re-orientation by remodelling simulation
approaches.method: The problem asks whether alignment is stronger than a load-independent growth rule would produce, but the size of that null is unknown. Simulate trabecular architecture on 2D and coarse 3D voxel domains (a femoral-head section and a rectangular block) under three rule families: (1) a Huiskes-type remodelling rule driven by strain energy density sensed by osteocytes with spatial influence decay; (2) load-independent rules (reaction-diffusion Turing-type patterning of bone deposition, and growth along a fixed developmental field such as radial distance from an ossification centre); (3) mixed rules with a tunable load weight w from 0 to 1. For each run compute the same fabric-to-principal-stress angle statistic as approach 1. Then rotate the applied load by 13 and 20 degrees, matching the magnitudes used in the guineafowl and sheep experiments (Pontzer et al. 2006; Barak et al. 2011), continue the simulation, and record the fabric re-orientation angle and its time constant.
steps: Implement the remodelling loop in Python with a voxel FE solver (FEniCSx or a sparse linear-elastic voxel solver), verify against the published qualitative outcomes of Huiskes et al. 2000 (aligned struts under uniaxial load, re-alignment after load rotation).
Implement the load-independent rules and the mixed-rule family; fix seeds and record all parameters.
For each rule and 20 seeds, compute the distribution of fabric-to-stress angles and the stress-anisotropy dependence.
Apply load rotation and record re-orientation angle versus simulated time.
Publish a lookup table: expected median angle and anisotropy slope for w in {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}, to be used as the pre-registered growth-rule null in approach 1.
approaches.decisive_result: A table showing that the alignment statistic separates load-driven (w = 1) from load-independent (w = 0) rules by more than the seed-to-seed spread, with the minimum load weight that produces a median angle below 20 degrees, and predicted re-orientation magnitudes for the two experimental rotations.
approaches.failure_signature: If load-independent rules on the same geometry produce median angles within the seed spread of the load-driven rule, the alignment statistic cannot discriminate causes and approach 1 must be redesigned around re-orientation; if results change by more than 10 degrees with voxel resolution or VOI size, the simulation is not converged.
approaches.missing: No wet data needed; this calibrates nulls and does not by itself settle whether real bone is aligned.

approaches.title: Lean proof that shear-driven rotation makes principal directions the stable fabric
approaches.method: Formalize the mechanism in claim thompson1917-ch16-06. For a plane stress state with principal stresses sigma1 > sigma2 and principal angle theta_p, the shear traction on a strut at angle theta is tau(theta) = ((sigma1 - sigma2)/2) sin(2(theta - theta_p)). Compare two rotation rules, k > 0. Rule A (signed shear): d theta/dt = -k tau(theta). Rule B (descent on shear energy): d theta/dt = -k d(tau^2)/d theta, which is proportional to -sin(4(theta - theta_p)). Prove: (i) under both rules the principal directions theta_p + m pi/2 are equilibria; (ii) under rule A the linearization -k(sigma1 - sigma2) cos(2(theta - theta_p)) is negative at theta_p and positive at theta_p + pi/2, so only one principal family is stable and Thompson's two orthogonal families (ch16-05) cannot both arise from it; (iii) under rule B both principal directions are asymptotically stable, the diagonals theta_p + pi/4 are the only other (unstable) equilibria, and V = tau^2 is a Lyapunov function non-increasing along trajectories; (iv) if sigma1 = sigma2 every angle is an equilibrium, so alignment is undefined under equal principal stresses. Part (ii)-(iii) says which reading of 'displaced by shear' is consistent with crossing tension and compression families; part (iv) yields the data prediction used in approach 1 that alignment strength should rise with stress anisotropy.
steps: Extend ThompsonLaws/Mechanics.lean with the shear traction formula derived from the existing stressAction (rotation of the symmetric tensor), proving tau is zero exactly on principal directions.
Prove the equilibrium characterization and the sign of the derivative at each equilibrium for rules A and B using Real.sin and Real.cos lemmas in Mathlib.
Prove V = tau^2 is non-increasing along any differentiable solution of rule B (HasDerivAt plus chain rule).
Prove the degenerate case sigma1 = sigma2.
Write the report entry under lean/reports with no sorry and standard axioms only, and link it to thompson1917-ch16-06.
approaches.decisive_result: A compiled Lean module with no sorry proving the four statements, recorded as formalized for thompson1917-ch16-06 in the lean reports, including the result that only the shear-energy rule makes both orthogonal families stable.
approaches.failure_signature: Needing a sorry for the stability or Lyapunov step, or a statement weakened to the point that it only restates tau = 0 on principal axes (already implied by the existing ch16-05 theorem).
approaches.missing: A proof shows the rule implies alignment, not that bone follows the rule; it does not address causality in organisms.

approaches.title: Meta-analysis of load-reorientation experiments for the causal arm
approaches.method: The causal falsifier (failure to re-orient after altered loading) can be tested on published experiments without new animals. Extract every controlled in vivo experiment in which joint load orientation or magnitude was changed and trabecular orientation measured against a control limb or group (starting with Pontzer et al. 2006 and Barak et al. 2011, plus studies found by a pre-registered search string in Europe PMC). The effect size is the change in primary fabric orientation in degrees relative to control, with the imposed load rotation as moderator. Fit a random-effects meta-regression of observed re-orientation on imposed rotation; Wolff's law predicts a slope near 1 (fabric tracks load) and an intercept near 0. Include studies with null results and record risk of bias (blinding, sample size).
steps: Pre-register the search string, inclusion criteria (controlled design, quantitative fabric angle, stated load-change angle) and the model.
Search Europe PMC and screen with two independent agents; resolve disagreements by a third.
Extract angles, SDs and n with page-level provenance; contact-free only, so studies without dispersion are recorded but excluded from pooling.
Fit the random-effects meta-regression (metafor, REML) and report the slope with 95% CI, heterogeneity I^2, and an Egger test.
approaches.decisive_result: Pooled slope of fabric re-orientation on imposed load rotation with 95% CI excluding 0 (causal tracking) and its distance from 1 (complete tracking), from at least five independent experiments.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than five eligible experiments, or a CI including 0, which would leave the causal claim unsupported; if eligible studies overwhelmingly report positive results with small n and Egger asymmetry, the pooled estimate is not credible.
approaches.missing: The number of controlled re-orientation experiments with extractable angles and dispersion may be below five; no wet lab to add new ones.

approaches.title: Blind stress-fabric alignment test across loaded bone sites
approaches.method: Scout intact, open micro-CT volumes for femoral head, vertebral body and calcaneus from at least two species, retaining only specimens for which defensible physiological boundary conditions can be fixed without viewing fabric orientation. Pre-register segmentation, mean-intercept-length fabric tensors in 5 mm-equivalent windows, linear-elastic finite elements, and the acute angle between the major fabric eigenvector and the nearest principal stress direction. Compare the observed median angle with 10,000 density-preserving random rotations and with a load-independent growth null fitted only to cortical shape and distance from surfaces; repeat over a predeclared ensemble of plausible load magnitudes without tuning directions.
steps: Scout and license-check at least three intact-bone datasets with metadata sufficient to define loads.
Freeze voxel-size, window-size, segmentation and finite-element convergence criteria before measuring alignment.
Compute specimen-level angular errors and null distributions with taxon and site as hierarchical effects.
Perform leave-one-site-out prediction and publish all meshes, load cases and randomization seeds.
approaches.decisive_result: For at least two of three sites, the pre-registered load case must yield a cross-specimen median angle at most 15 degrees and at least 10 degrees below both null medians, with a 95% hierarchical interval excluding zero; otherwise stress alignment is not supported at the stated tolerance.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than three usable paired geometry/load datasets, mesh non-convergence, or angular advantage under 10 degrees over either null shows that the approach cannot resolve the claim as stated.
approaches.missing: Paired open whole-bone micro-CT and independently justified physiological load metadata may not exist for three sites; scouting must establish this before preregistration.

approaches.title: Out-of-sample load inference from trabecular architecture
approaches.method: Turn the potentially circular agreement test into a prediction task. For each scanned bone, define a finite library of anatomically plausible load directions before inspecting trabecular fabric. Fit a mechanostat-remodelling model and a load-independent reaction-diffusion growth model on training specimens, then ask each model to rank the held-out specimen's true load direction from architecture alone. Use the same density field and material law in both models, and score top-one identification plus angular error; this tests whether stress leaves information in architecture that a developmental null does not.
steps: Generate preregistered candidate load libraries and synthetic recovery tests.
Calibrate remodelling and developmental-null parameters only on training specimens.
Blind the held-out load label and rank candidate directions by posterior predictive discrepancy.
Repeat leave-one-specimen-out and report sensitivity to material anisotropy and boundary conditions.
approaches.decisive_result: Stress causation gains support if the remodelling model identifies the held-out load within 15 degrees in at least 80% of at least 20 specimens and exceeds the developmental null by at least 25 percentage points with a permutation p-value below 0.05.
approaches.failure_signature: Equivalent predictive accuracy of the two models, strong dependence on a tuned boundary condition, or failure on synthetic recovery falsifies the proposed discriminator.
approaches.missing: A public set of at least 20 specimens with known loading class is not yet established; static architecture cannot directly test reorientation after altered loading.

approaches.title: Mean-intercept fabric versus finite-element principal stress
approaches.method: Pre-register a claim test of thompson1917-ch16-05 before any orientation or stress field is inspected. In each surviving volume, binarize bone with Otsu's threshold on the bone histogram and compute the mean-intercept-length fabric tensor on a grid of cubic regions of interest (BoneJ anisotropy, or an equivalent coded intercept count). The stress tensor comes from a linear-elastic finite-element solve on the same geometry with one isotropic tissue modulus, so the fabric never enters the stress calculation. The primary load cases, fixed in advance, are: femoral head, uniform pressure on a spherical cap of 40 degree half-angle directed from the articular surface through the head centre toward the neck, distal cut fixed; vertebral body, uniform compression of the endplates. The statistic is the angle between the undirected primary fabric axis and the principal-stress direction of largest absolute value, folded into 0 to 90 degrees. The random-fabric null keeps the measured eigenvalues and draws the primary axis uniformly; for that null the distribution is known, P(angle ≤ θ) = 1 − cos θ on [0, π/2], so the null median is 60 degrees, and the script checks the formula with a Monte Carlo of the same draws. The growth-rule null aligns fabric with the local density gradient, or with the scanner superior-inferior axis when that gradient is below a pre-registered magnitude. A volume is dropped if it is an excised cube whose anatomical orientation is not in the deposit, if trabecular thickness is under three voxels, or if the growth-rule axis cannot be defined. Pass requires, on at least three volumes from at least two species, a median angle ≤ 20 degrees that is also at least 15 degrees below both null medians, with a permutation p < 0.01. A pre-registered cap-angle sweep from 20 to 60 degrees tests the load-case falsifier: a change under 5 degrees that leaves the median inside the random-fabric null counts as insensitive to the load.
steps: Write the pre-registration (thresholds, load cases, exclusion gates) and commit it before downloading volumes.
Download the Leeds lumbar set, the unaugmented Palanca vertebrae, the DaRUS femoral-head overview, and only those Doube stacks whose filenames and the 2011 protocol identify a whole head or condyle.
Apply the resolution and orientation gates; record every exclusion.
Compute mean-intercept-length fabric and the finite-element principal stresses on the surviving volumes.
Compare angles with the random-axis null and the growth-rule null, then run the cap-angle sweep.
approaches.decisive_result: A table of fabric-to-stress angles for every surviving region, with the median ≤ 20 degrees and at least 15 degrees below both null medians at permutation p < 0.01, on at least three volumes from two species. The cap-angle sweep must move the median by at least 5 degrees or the load-case falsifier trips.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than three volumes survive the gates; the median is not distinguishable from the random-fabric null (median 60 degrees); or the median moves by less than 5 degrees across the cap-angle sweep while remaining inside that null.
approaches.missing: Subject-specific joint loads are not in these deposits, and many Doube volumes are excised cubes. The test uses stated load cases and drops cubes whose orientation is unrecorded. No animal lab is available for a new reorientation experiment.

approaches.title: Stress-adaptive remodelling versus a load-independent rule
approaches.method: This attacks the mechanism in thompson1917-ch16-06 and the reorientation prediction in thompson1917-ch16-07 as a sufficiency question, not as a substitute for the micro-CT test. On a 2D plane-stress mesh of a cantilever and of a femoral-head silhouette, iterate a Huiskes-type density update: the strain-energy density is recomputed by linear finite elements each step, and density grows where strain energy per unit density exceeds a reference value, with a lazy zone of ±10 percent inside which density does not change. The comparison rule uses the same update but drives it with a fixed anatomical gradient and never with stress. After a pre-registered iteration budget, compute the mean-intercept fabric of the density field and its angle to the principal stress of the final solid. Then rotate the load by 30 degrees and continue. A bounded Frontier mechanobiology preview may smoke-test one parameter set; it is not the result, because those previews are not accepted evidence.
steps: Freeze the two update rules, the lazy-zone width, the mesh and the iteration budget before any production run.
Run the stress rule and the gradient rule from the same initial density.
Measure fabric-to-stress angle at convergence.
Rotate the load by 30 degrees and record the fabric rotation.
Repeat from three initial densities to separate the rule from the initial condition.
approaches.decisive_result: Under the stress rule the median fabric-to-stress angle is ≤ 15 degrees, and after the 30 degree load rotation the fabric axis turns by ≥ 20 degrees. The gradient rule stays above 40 degrees from the principal stress. Both comparisons hold for all three initial densities.
approaches.failure_signature: The stress rule does not beat the gradient rule by 15 degrees, the density collapses to empty or solid, or the iteration oscillates past the budget without a fabric axis stable to 5 degrees.

approaches.title: Lean: shear vanishes only on principal planes
approaches.method: Thompson's reason for alignment, in thompson1917-ch16-06, is that a plane along a principal direction carries no shear. The repo already proves that principal directions of a 2D symmetric stress are orthogonal (ThompsonLaws.Mechanics.principalDirections_orthogonal). Extend that file. For the stress [[a, b], [b, c]] and a unit normal, define the shear component of the traction and prove it is zero if and only if the normal is an eigenvector, when the two principal values are distinct. Then prove the alignment lemma used as the optimality piece: for a fixed stress with distinct eigenvalues, the Frobenius product with a fabric of fixed eigenvalues is maximised exactly when the eigenframes coincide. In 2D that product is a cos 2θ + b sin 2θ, and the maximum is at θ = 0. The development stays in 2D plane stress so it can close on the existing lemma. It does not say that bone does this.
steps: Define traction and its shear part for a 2D symmetric stress.
Prove shear vanishes if and only if the normal is a principal direction.
Prove the 2D Frobenius product is maximised when the frames coincide.
Build the Thompson Lake project with no sorry and only standard axioms.
approaches.decisive_result: A Lean module, compiled with no sorry, containing both the shear characterisation and the 2D alignment-maximum theorem.
approaches.failure_signature: Either theorem still contains sorry, or the alignment statement is true only after assuming something the mechanics lemma does not give (a nonsymmetric stress, or a 3D spectral theorem the development does not have).

problems.title: Does hierarchy itself explain the toughness of biological composites?
problems.question: Across nacre, bone, dentin, antler and other mineralised composites, is fracture toughness predicted by quantitative structural descriptors (mineral volume fraction, platelet aspect ratio, interface compliance, number of hierarchical levels) beyond what the constituents' stiffness and strength predict? Is there a scaling of toughness enhancement with the number of hierarchical levels?
problems.known_state: Natural composites reach toughness well above that of their brittle mineral phase (Launey and Ritchie 2009; Wegst et al. 2015). Nacre's tablets and soft interlayer have been modelled as a tension-shear chain and measured at the tablet scale (Jackson, Vincent and Turner 1988; Barthelat et al. 2007), and interface mechanics is reviewed by Barthelat et al. 2016. Ashby, Gibson, Wegst and Olive 1995 chart property ranges of natural materials. What is missing is a single dataset-wide regression that separates the contribution of architecture from constituents, and a test of whether toughness gain compounds with hierarchical levels as often asserted. Thompson's claim (ch. 16-02) that bone is an economical material is the starting point for the bone case.
acceptance_criteria: A pre-registered meta-analysis of at least 40 published material records spanning at least five biocomposite families, with structural descriptors extracted by stated rules, the null model (constituent-only mixing law) and the toughness-enhancement metric fixed in advance, and a leave-one-family-out validation.
falsifiers: If a constituent-only model explains the toughness within the stated error bound, hierarchy adds nothing and the claim is refuted for this dataset.
If enhancement is not monotone in the number of hierarchical levels after controlling for volume fraction, the compounding claim is refuted.
problems.data_access: Published material property tables and supplementary data (Ashby et al. 1995 charts, Wegst et al. 2015 and Barthelat et al. 2016 compilations, tablet-scale nacre measurements); records have to be extracted with provenance and each family's measurement method checked, because fracture toughness methods differ between papers.

related_claims.label: Bone is nearly as strong in tension as in compression
Skeletal form is largely a diagram of mechanical stress

approaches.title: Pre-registered meta-regression of toughness enhancement over a constituent-only bound
approaches.method: Build a provenanced table of at least 40 records across at least five families (nacre, bone by site, dentin, enamel, antler, crustacean cuticle, sponge spicule) from primary papers cited in the Wegst 2015, Launey and Ritchie 2009, Barthelat 2016 and Ritchie 2011 reviews. Fix the toughness metric first: crack-initiation toughness K_IC and, separately, the maximum crack-growth toughness from J-R curves converted to K_J = sqrt(J E'), because hierarchy acts mostly on extrinsic crack-growth toughening and pooling the two would blur the effect. The constituent-only null is an energy mixing law G_mix = phi G_mineral + (1 - phi) G_organic with E from the Voigt-Reuss average, K_mix = sqrt(E_mix G_mix). The enhancement metric is log(K / K_mix). Regress it on platelet or fibril aspect ratio, mineral volume fraction, interface compliance proxy (organic layer thickness over platelet thickness) and the number of hierarchical levels counted by a written rule (a level counts only if it has its own characteristic length differing by at least a factor 5 from adjacent levels and its own documented deformation mechanism), with family as random effect. Validate by leave-one-family-out prediction.
steps: Pre-register metric definitions, extraction rules, the level-counting rule, the model and the pass thresholds in test-data/claim-tests.
Extract records with page and table provenance; two independent agents per record, discrepancies adjudicated.
Compute K_mix from constituent values reported in the same paper where possible, else from a fixed reference table of mineral and collagen/chitin properties stated in advance.
Fit mixed models: null (intercept only, i.e. constituents explain toughness up to a constant), architecture model, levels model; compare by leave-one-family-out RMSE.
Test monotonicity of enhancement in levels with an isotonic regression versus a flat model, controlling for volume fraction.
approaches.decisive_result: Leave-one-family-out RMSE of the architecture model at least 25% lower than the constituent-only null on log enhancement, and the level coefficient positive with 95% CI excluding 0 after controlling for volume fraction (compounding supported), or not (compounding refuted).
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than five families with both toughness and descriptors from comparable test methods; level counts that change under reasonable alternative counting rules (sensitivity analysis flips the sign); or measurement method (specimen size, hydration) explaining more variance than any structural descriptor.
approaches.missing: Interface compliance and constituent toughness are rarely measured in the same study as composite toughness; hydration state and test geometry differ between papers and cannot be harmonized without new measurements.

approaches.title: Simulated fracture of self-similar staggered composites with 1 to 4 levels
approaches.method: Settle the compounding question in a model where constituents are held exactly fixed, which no dataset allows. Build 2D lattice-spring (or discrete-element beam) fracture models of the tension-shear staggered architecture (Ji and Gao 2004; Gao et al. 2003): level 1 is mineral platelets in a soft matrix; level n replaces each platelet of level n-1 with a scaled-up copy of the level n-1 composite, keeping the total mineral fraction fixed. Mineral and matrix springs have fixed stiffness and brittle failure strains. Load notched specimens in mode I to compute work of fracture and the resistance curve. Vary aspect ratio and mineral fraction at each level; compare against a single-level composite with the same total mineral fraction and against a random (non-staggered) arrangement of the same phases.
steps: Implement a 2D quasi-static lattice-spring fracture code (Python with sparse solvers), validated on the analytic tension-shear chain stiffness formula for level 1.
Generate hierarchical geometries for n = 1..4 at fixed total phi, with 20 random realizations each (platelet offset jitter).
Run notched fracture tests; record peak load, work of fracture, R-curve slope; check mesh and specimen-size convergence (specimen at least 10 times the largest level length).
Fit enhancement versus n and test monotonicity and saturation (isotonic versus logistic-saturation fit).
Write the predicted enhancement-per-level curve as the quantitative prior for approach 1's levels coefficient.
approaches.decisive_result: Curve of work-of-fracture enhancement versus number of levels at fixed constituents with realization-level 95% CIs, showing whether enhancement is monotone, saturating or non-monotone, and its sensitivity to aspect ratio.
approaches.failure_signature: Results that change by more than the realization spread when specimen size or lattice resolution changes (size effect not controlled), making the levels comparison an artefact; or failure to reproduce the level-1 analytic stiffness within 5%.
approaches.missing: A 2D spring model omits 3D crack deflection and twisting and fibril-level plasticity; it answers the compounding question for the model, not for real tissues.

approaches.title: Lean bounds: hierarchy cannot raise stiffness past the Voigt bound
approaches.method: Separate what hierarchy can and cannot do. Formalize the tension-shear chain effective modulus 1/E = 4(1 - phi)/(G_p phi^2 rho^2) + 1/(phi E_m) (Gao et al. 2003, with rho the aspect ratio, G_p the matrix shear modulus and E_m the mineral modulus) and prove: (i) E is increasing in rho and bounded above by phi E_m; (ii) applying the formula recursively, with level n using the level n-1 modulus as its 'mineral', the modulus at every level is bounded by the Voigt bound of the total mineral fraction, so stiffness cannot compound with levels; (iii) the strength of the level-n composite is bounded by the mineral strength times the total volume fraction under the same chain model. The result sharpens the problem: any compounding must be in toughness (energy dissipation), which is where the data test and the simulation should look, and claims of compounding stiffness or strength are refuted by the model itself.
steps: Write ThompsonLaws/Biocomposite.lean defining the chain modulus and the recursive hierarchy.
Prove monotonicity in rho and the upper bound phi E_m (field_simp, positivity, div_le_iff).
Prove the recursive bound by induction on the level, with total fraction the product of per-level fractions.
Prove the strength bound under the stated load-transfer assumptions.
Record in lean/reports and link to thompson1917-ch16-02 as a supporting formal statement, not as a proof of the claim.
approaches.decisive_result: Compiled Lean module with no sorry stating the stiffness and strength bounds for arbitrary numbers of levels.
approaches.failure_signature: The recursive bound requires assumptions (e.g. matrix shear modulus scaling across levels) that cannot be stated without making the theorem vacuous.

approaches.title: Measurement-aware leave-family-out toughness meta-analysis
approaches.method: Build a provenance-locked table of at least 40 records from nacre, cortical bone, dentin, antler and one additional mineralized composite. Record crack orientation, specimen dimensions, toughness protocol, hydration, mineral fraction, constituent moduli and strengths, platelet or fibril aspect ratio, interface compliance and a rule-based count of hierarchical levels. Fit a constituent-only mixing-law baseline and a hierarchical model with protocol-specific measurement error; test architecture by leave-one-family-out prediction rather than in-sample significance.
steps: Publish an extraction codebook and dual-extract a 20% paper sample before resolving disagreements.
Convert toughness measures only where standards make them commensurable; otherwise model protocol strata separately.
Fit constituent-only, descriptor and hierarchy-count models with family-level random effects.
Run leave-one-family-out prediction and a monotonicity test for hierarchy count.
approaches.decisive_result: Architecture explains a dataset-wide effect if the descriptor model reduces held-out log-toughness RMSE by at least 20% versus the constituent-only model in at least four of five held-out families; compounding requires a positive hierarchy-count coefficient whose 95% interval excludes zero after all controls.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than 40 commensurable records, no held-out RMSE gain, or a hierarchy-count interval containing zero defeats the corresponding claim.
approaches.missing: The records are scattered and fracture-toughness protocols are heterogeneous; enough commensurable open records may not survive the exclusion rules.

approaches.title: Factorial fracture simulation isolates hierarchy from constituents
approaches.method: Construct a two-dimensional discrete cohesive-zone model with identical mineral fraction, constituent elastic laws and interface fracture energy across designs. Enumerate single-level brick-and-mortar, two-level nested and three-level nested architectures over platelet aspect ratio and interface-compliance grids. Match total mass and smallest feature size, compute J-integral or work-to-failure under mode-I and mixed-mode loading, and use a factorial decomposition to estimate the pure hierarchy interaction after controlling for tortuosity and interface area.
steps: Validate the solver against analytic laminate and single-crack limits.
Generate matched architectures over a preregistered parameter grid with mesh-convergence checks.
Compute peak stress, work-to-failure and crack-path tortuosity under two loading modes.
Fit a response surface and locate regions where adding a level helps, harms or is neutral.
approaches.decisive_result: Hierarchy compounds toughness in the model only if each added level raises median work-to-failure by at least 25% at fixed constituents, mass, interface area and minimum feature size across at least 75% of the preregistered parameter grid.
approaches.failure_signature: No mesh-converged gain, gains attributable entirely to extra interface area, or frequent decreases after adding levels refutes a generic hierarchy effect in this model class.
approaches.missing: This settles a controlled theoretical piece, not whether real tissues occupy the beneficial parameter region; three-dimensional validation would require more compute and measurements.

approaches.title: Leave-one-family regression of toughness on architecture
approaches.method: Build a provenanced table of published fracture records for mineralised composites, aimed at the problem's bar of at least 40 records and five families (nacre, bone, dentin, antler, and one of enamel, sea-urchin stereom or stomatopod cuticle). Each row records the family, the toughness quantity and the method name, mineral volume fraction, mineral Young's modulus, mineral strength, platelet or fibril aspect ratio, an interface-compliance proxy defined as organic-layer thickness divided by platelet thickness, and the number of hierarchical levels counted by a written rule (a level counts only if the paper names a distinct structural element at that scale). Work of fracture is not pooled with K_Ic. The constituent-only null, fixed first, is log10(K_Ic) = a + b φ + c log10(E_mineral) + d log10(σ_mineral) + error. The architecture model adds log10(aspect ratio), log10(interface compliance) and the level count N. Pass requires a likelihood-ratio test of those three terms at p < 0.01, and a leave-one-family-out check in which the architecture model cuts mean absolute error on log10(K_Ic) by at least 0.10 relative to the null in at least four of five held-out families. Compounding is a separate coefficient: N has a positive coefficient whose 95 percent interval excludes zero in the model that already contains φ. Rows missing a required field are dropped, not imputed.
steps: Write the extraction rules, the level-counting rule and both model formulas before reading tables for the purpose of fitting.
Extract records from open papers and from supplements, keeping the page or table for each number.
Drop rows that mix toughness definitions or lack a required field.
Fit the null and the architecture model; run the likelihood-ratio test and leave-one-family-out.
Report the coefficient on N after controlling for mineral volume fraction.
approaches.decisive_result: At least 40 K_Ic records, five families, a likelihood-ratio p < 0.01 for the architecture block, a leave-one-family-out error drop of at least 0.10 log10 units in at least four families, and a 95 percent interval for the level-count coefficient that lies entirely above zero. Anything short of the coverage bar is a failed test, not a fit on a smaller table.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than 40 complete K_Ic records or fewer than five families remain after the method filter; the likelihood-ratio test is above 0.01; or the level-count interval includes zero or is negative, which refutes compounding even if the joint architecture test passes.
approaches.missing: There is no open database that already joins toughness with aspect ratio, interface compliance and level count. Several source papers are paywalled, and interface thickness is often unreported, so the table may miss the coverage bar.

approaches.title: Self-similar hierarchy sweep of toughness against level count
approaches.method: Transcribe the quasi-self-similar tension-shear recurrence of Zhang, Zhang and Gao 2011 from the paper's equations, not from memory of their plotted optimum. Sweep mineral volume fraction from 0.05 to 0.95 and the matrix failure shear strain over the factor-of-two box around the values printed in that paper. At each point compute stiffness, strength and toughness at hierarchy levels N = 1 through 8 under the equal-strength closure, and again with a weakest-link flaw inserted at the largest level. The compounding claim is that toughness keeps rising with N. The pre-registered window is N = 2 through 7 and mineral fraction 0.30 to 0.95. Compounding survives this model only if toughness is increasing throughout that window for every parameter point in the box.
steps: Code the recurrence so that it matches the paper's equations line by line, with a unit test against one printed numerical example if the paper gives one.
Sweep volume fraction and matrix failure strain.
Record toughness against N and the smallest N at which the first difference becomes negative.
Repeat with the weakest-link flaw at the top level.
Archive the curves and the parameter box.
approaches.decisive_result: The curve of toughness against N, and the set of volume fractions for which the first difference changes from positive to negative inside N = 2 through 7. Compounding is supported only if no such sign change occurs anywhere in the pre-registered box.
approaches.failure_signature: No stationary point of toughness exists for any volume fraction in [0.05, 0.95], or the sign pattern reverses when the equal-strength closure is replaced by the weakest-link flaw, so the monotone-or-not answer is an artefact of one closure.

approaches.title: Lean proof that the transcribed toughness recurrence is not monotone
approaches.method: Take the same recurrence used in the sweep and define it in Lean as a function of level, volume fraction and the matrix parameters. Prove two algebraic facts, and nothing about continuum fracture. First, stiffness at level n is at most the Voigt bound set by the mineral fraction, so adding a level cannot raise stiffness above that bound. Second, there exists an open set of positive parameters on which toughness at level n+1 is strictly less than toughness at level n for some n ≤ 7. The second statement is the negation of unrestricted compounding. The proof obligation is the paper's recurrence as transcribed; if the transcription disagrees with the paper, the theorem is void rather than patched.
steps: Define the recurrence in ThompsonLaws as a pure function of the paper's parameters.
Prove the Voigt upper bound on stiffness under that recurrence.
Exhibit a rational parameter point, checked in the proof, where toughness falls between two successive levels.
Compile with no sorry.
approaches.decisive_result: A sorry-free Lean theorem that the transcribed recurrence is not monotone in the level count on a nonempty open set of positive parameters, together with the stiffness bound.
approaches.failure_signature: The recurrence cannot be stated in Lean without extra scaling assumptions that make the decrease trivial, or the transcribed equations do not match Zhang, Zhang and Gao 2011, or sorry remains.

problems.title: Are biological hollow structures at the stiffness-per-mass optimum?
problems.question: For bone shafts, plant stems, bamboo, feathers and quills, is the radius-to-wall-thickness ratio at the value that maximizes bending stiffness per unit mass, or does a competing constraint (local buckling, impact, vascular space, growth) set it? How large is the systematic deviation, and does it depend on the organism's size?
problems.known_state: Thompson (1917, ch. 16) argues that where stiffness against bending in all directions is required organisms use hollow cylinders with little material in the core, and that the walls of long bones are thickest where bending is greatest. Thin-walled-tube theory gives the stiffness-per-mass optimum and the local-buckling limit, and Ashby, Gibson, Wegst and Olive 1995 compare natural and engineering shapes. We know of no pre-registered cross-taxon comparison of measured thickness ratios with the optimum and buckling limits that uses the measured material properties of each structure, so the extent of optimality is unmeasured.
acceptance_criteria: A pre-registered comparison of measured radius and wall thickness for at least 100 structures from at least four structure types (long bones, stems, bamboo culms, feather rachises), each with its measured tissue modulus, against the stiffness-per-mass optimum and the buckling limit, with the tolerance for 'at optimum' stated in advance.
falsifiers: If the measured ratios cluster at the buckling limit rather than at the stiffness-per-mass optimum for most structures, the optimality claim is refuted and a buckling-limited design is supported.
If the ratios show no relation to either, the claim is refuted for the tested set.
problems.data_access: Published cross-section morphometry of long bones, culms and rachises, and open CT of limb bones on MorphoSource; tissue modulus values have to be taken from the same or a closely matched source, which limits the usable sample.

related_claims.label: Structures that must resist bending are built as hollow tubes
Femoral wall thickness follows the bending-moment distribution along the shaft

approaches.title: Formalize the constrained optimum: empty tubes have none, filled tubes do
approaches.method: The question presupposes an interior stiffness-per-mass optimum, but for an empty thin-walled tube at fixed mass (fixed r t) the bending stiffness E pi r^3 t grows as r^2, so stiffness per mass increases without bound as K = r_inner/r_outer goes to 1 and only local buckling (Brazier ovalisation, whose collapse moment scales as E r t^2 / sqrt(1 - nu^2)) or another constraint stops it. With a marrow or pith core of density ratio q = rho_core/rho_wall that must be carried, Currey and Alexander (1985) showed an interior optimum K*(q) exists. Formalize: (i) for an empty tube, stiffness-per-mass at fixed outer radius is strictly increasing in K on [0, 1); (ii) with core mass included, the mass at fixed bending stiffness has a unique minimum K*(q) in (0, 1) for q in (0, 1), and K* decreases as q increases; (iii) under a Brazier constraint the feasible set is K <= K_b(E, sigma_allow), so the predicted K is min(K*(q), K_b). These three lemmas turn the vague 'optimum' into three numerical predictions per structure: pneumatic (q = 0) structures should sit at the buckling limit, filled structures at K*(q).
steps: Define I(K) = (pi/4) R^4 (1 - K^4), wall area pi R^2 (1 - K^2), core area pi R^2 K^2 in Lean.
Prove the empty-tube monotonicity lemma.

Prove existence and uniqueness of the minimum-mass K* at fixed stiffness for core density ratio q in (0,1), via the derivative sign or an explicit convexity argument after the substitution x = K^2, and the monotone dependence on q.
State the Brazier feasibility constraint as a hypothesis-parameterized inequality and prove the min rule.
Compute K*(q) numerically for q in the range of marrow (fatty and haematopoietic) and pith densities, and store the table for approach 2.
approaches.decisive_result: Compiled Lean module with no sorry proving the three lemmas, plus a numeric K*(q) table that makes the data test's predictions explicit.
approaches.failure_signature: Uniqueness of K* cannot be proved without restricting q to a narrower interval than real marrow and pith densities span, in which case the prediction is not well defined for some structures.

approaches.title: Cross-taxon test of K against marrow-adjusted optimum and buckling limit
approaches.method: Compile at least 100 structures from four types: marrow-filled mammal long bones, pneumatic and marrow-filled bird long bones, bamboo culms and hollow grass stems, and feather rachises, each with outer radius, wall thickness and tissue modulus from the same or a matched source. For each, compute three predictions from approach 1: K*(q) (core-mass-adjusted stiffness optimum), K_b (Brazier local-buckling limit using measured E and an assumed strength-to-modulus ratio stated per tissue) and the predicted value min(K*, K_b). The sharpest test is within birds: pneumatic bones carry no marrow mass, so they are predicted to sit nearer K_b, while marrow-filled bones of the same birds should sit near K*(q). Classify each structure as at-optimum (|K - K*| <= 0.05), at-buckling (|K - K_b| <= 0.05), or neither; test size dependence by regressing K on log body or structure mass with phylogenetic GLS for the animal subset.
steps: Pre-register the tolerance (0.05 in K), the q values per tissue, and the classification rule.
Extract K and E from Currey and Alexander 1985 and other primary tables found by a pre-registered search; resolve taxa through the organisms layer (GBIF, NCBI).
Compute predictions and classify; run the paired pneumatic-versus-marrow comparison with a sign test and a mixed model with species as random effect.
Fit K versus log mass, phylogenetically corrected for vertebrates.
