approaches.decisive_result: Proportions of structures at K*, at K_b and at neither, with the pneumatic-versus-filled contrast in birds; Thompson's optimality claim is supported if most filled structures fall within 0.05 of K* and pneumatic ones are shifted toward K_b.
approaches.failure_signature: Most structures fall in the 'neither' class, or the pneumatic-filled contrast is absent or reversed; or fewer than 100 structures have a matched modulus, in which case the test is underpowered rather than decisive.
approaches.missing: Matched tissue moduli for feather rachises and many plant stems are sparse; bird pneumaticity status per bone must be extracted from anatomical literature.

approaches.title: Measure K along the shaft from open CT and test the bending-moment profile
approaches.method: Use open CT of limb bones (MorphoSource, with licences recorded) to measure K and cortical thickness at 5% increments along the diaphysis in at least 60 bones across mammals and birds spanning three orders of magnitude in body mass. This gives both a size-dependent test of K at mid-shaft and a direct test of the companion claim thompson1917-ch16-04 (already formalized in Lean as uniformStressThickness_max_mid): wall thickness should track the bending-moment profile of a stated load case. Segment cortical bone with a fixed threshold, compute second moments of area and K per slice, and regress the thickness profile on the bending-moment profile of a three-point-bending load case with the actual bone length.
steps: Scout MorphoSource for open-download femora and humeri with voxel size below 1% of shaft diameter; record licences.
Pre-register slice spacing, threshold rule, load case and the pass criterion (Pearson r >= 0.7 between thickness and moment profiles in most bones; mid-shaft K within 0.05 of K*(q) from approach 1).
Run segmentation and cross-section geometry (BoneJ slice geometry).
Fit K versus log body mass with phylogenetic GLS; report the thickness-moment correlation per bone.
approaches.decisive_result: Distribution of mid-shaft K versus body mass and of the thickness-to-moment correlation across at least 60 bones, against the pre-registered thresholds.
approaches.failure_signature: Thickness profiles that peak away from mid-shaft in most bones (e.g. near muscle insertions), or too few open-download specimens to span the mass range.
approaches.missing: Many MorphoSource specimens require download requests; bone-specific load cases are approximations.

approaches.title: Formal Pareto envelope for hollow tubes with buckling constraints
approaches.method: State the circular-annulus optimization exactly: for fixed material area and length, derive second moment of area as a function of outer and inner radii, then add local shell buckling, Euler buckling and maximum-radius constraints. Prove in Lean 4 that unconstrained bending stiffness increases as material moves outward, that no finite wall-thickness optimum exists without an added constraint, and that the constrained optimum lies on at least one active buckling or radius boundary. Numerically map the resulting nondimensional Pareto envelope in slenderness, modulus and load.
steps: Define annular area, second moment, bending stiffness and nondimensional geometry in Lean.
Prove monotonicity at fixed area and existence of a constrained maximizer on a compact feasible set.
Prove the active-constraint lemma and verify symbolic special cases.
Generate a numerical envelope that converts measured radius, thickness and load into optimality gap.
approaches.decisive_result: A no-sorry Lean module proving the monotonicity, existence and active-constraint lemmas, plus a reproducible envelope, settles what 'stiffness-per-mass optimum' can mathematically mean and shows whether buckling is required to define a finite optimum.
approaches.failure_signature: A counterexample to the active-constraint lemma or an unavoidable unsupported shell-buckling axiom means the formal route has not established the claimed optimum.

approaches.title: Cross-structure distance to the constrained tube optimum
approaches.method: Measure outer radius, wall-thickness distribution, length and ovality from at least 100 published cross-sections spanning long bones, bamboo or grass culms, stems and feather rachises. Use modulus and failure-property values from the same specimen or narrowly matched tissue, propagate those uncertainties through the formal Pareto envelope, and estimate each structure's log-distance from bending-optimal, local-buckling and Euler-buckling boundaries. Pre-register structure type, body size and safety factor as predictors in a hierarchical model.
steps: Scout records and freeze matching rules for geometry, material properties and loads.
Segment cross-sections with blinded duplicate measurements on 10% of records.
Compute uncertainty distributions over the three candidate constraint boundaries.
Fit type-specific and allometric models and perform leave-one-type-out validation.
approaches.decisive_result: A constraint explains a structure type if at least 70% of its records lie within 20% of that boundary and are at least twice as far from each competing boundary; otherwise that type is not classified as mechanically optimal under the model.
approaches.failure_signature: Insufficient matched material properties, no concentration near any boundary, or classification reversal under plausible loads refutes the cross-taxon optimum claim.
approaches.missing: Same-specimen loads and tissue moduli are uncommon, especially for feathers and plants, and may reduce the admissible sample below 100.

approaches.title: Lean: a gas-filled tube has no interior stiffness optimum
approaches.method: For a circular tube, k = r_inner / r_outer in [0, 1). With the second moment of area held fixed, bone cross-sectional area is proportional to sqrt((1 − k^2) / (1 + k^2)). Prove in Lean that this factor is strictly decreasing in k, so with a weightless core the stiffness-per-mass minimum is the thin-wall limit and there is no interior optimum. That is the content of the gas-filled case of Currey and Alexander's mass argument, derived here rather than quoted as a number. Then define total mass per unit length with a core density ratio q = ρ_core / ρ_bone, μ(k) = (1 − k^2 + q k^2) times the radius factor required by the fixed second moment. Prove the critical-point equation obtained by differentiating μ, and prove that a critical point in (0, 1) exists only for q in an interval the proof identifies. Local buckling enters as a symbolic lower bound t/R ≥ C σ/E; the constrained optimum is the unconstrained critical point if it satisfies the inequality, and the boundary otherwise. The constant C stays a parameter. thompson1917-ch16-04 already has the uniform-stress thickness in Lean; this approach does not redo that theorem.
steps: Define k, the fixed-second-moment area and μ(k, q) in ThompsonLaws.
Prove the gas-core area is strictly decreasing in k.
Derive and prove the stationarity condition for q > 0.
State the buckling constraint symbolically and the constrained argmin.
Compile with no sorry.
approaches.decisive_result: Sorry-free theorems: gas-core area decreases strictly in k, and the core-density stationarity condition together with the interval of q on which an interior minimum exists.
approaches.failure_signature: The gas-core monotonicity proof does not close, or differentiation of μ produces no interior critical point for any q, in which case the lemma is wrong and must not be restated to force a minimum.

approaches.title: Measured hollowness against the mass optimum and buckling
approaches.method: Using the k-star and the buckling boundary from the Lean development, compare measured hollowness on every open record that supplies either an inner and outer radius or the two areas that define them. For a circular annulus, global compactness Cg = bone area / total area gives k = sqrt(1 − Cg). Amson and Bibi deposit humeral MeanArea, MeanC, cross-sectional shape and body mass for 152 mammal species (159 rows in the humerus file). MeanC is used as compactness only if their methods equate it with Cg; otherwise those rows are dropped from the k test and MeanArea is not a substitute. Alfieri, Nyakatura and Amson deposit cortical compactness and cortical area for humeri and femora of slow arboreal mammals, a lifestyle-biased long-bone set. The junco deposit has cortical thickness, total area and marrow area for femur and humerus of one species, which determine k directly. Bamboo is the one verified culm table with outer diameter and wall thickness on some internodes, plus the single Moso culm whose diameters and mean wall thickness are stated in Dixon and Gibson. Feather rachises are included only from the measurements printed in the 2017 Royal Society Open Science rachis paper, and only if that supplement can be fetched. A structure is at the stiffness optimum if |k − k-star(q)| ≤ 0.10, and at the buckling limit if it is within 0.10 of the buckling boundary and farther than 0.10 from k-star. The core ratio q is 0 for air-filled culms and pneumatic bones, and is the marrow-to-bone density ratio only when a fetched source states it. Tissue modulus must come from the same paper or the row is excluded from the buckling comparison. The problem's bar is at least 100 structures of at least four types; this approach reports that count and does not relax it.
steps: Pre-register the 0.10 bands, the circular-annulus conversion and the rule for q before converting any table.
Confirm from Amson and Bibi's methods whether MeanC is global compactness; drop it if not.
Compute k for every row with a verified radius pair or area pair.
Attach a modulus only from the same paper, then classify each row.
Test whether the majority class is the stiffness optimum, the buckling boundary, or neither, by structure type.
approaches.decisive_result: A classification of at least 100 structures from four types (long bones, stems, bamboo culms, feather rachises), each with a matched modulus, into at-optimum, at-buckling or neither, using the 0.10 bands. The optimality claim passes only if the majority of structures in most types are at-optimum rather than at-buckling.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than four types have at least ten modulus-matched structures, so the acceptance bar is missed; or the measured k values fall mostly in neither class; or they cluster on the buckling boundary rather than on k-star.
approaches.missing: No public stem radius-and-wall compilation was verified. The feather paper's publisher page blocked a scripted fetch, so its table may be unreachable. Matched tissue moduli are missing for most long-bone rows, and the swarm has no calipers or scanner of its own.

approaches.title: Plot every measured tube on the mass and buckling curves
approaches.method: Even if the four-type bar fails, the mass curve itself can be drawn for every structure that has both k and a same-paper modulus. Evaluate μ(k) from the Lean definition at fixed second moment, for q = 0 and for the marrow ratio if one has been fetched, and draw the buckling boundary t/R = C σ/E with C symbolic at three stated values (the value read from Gibson, Ashby, Wegst and Olive 1995 if the fetched text gives it, otherwise the three placeholders 0.1, 0.3 and 1 are not used; the script plots the boundary as a function of C and does not pick a favourite after seeing the data). Place each measured (k, E) on that plot. This computation does not declare the biological claim settled when n is small. It does say, for the structures in hand, whether they sit nearer the descending mass curve's thin-wall end or nearer a buckling boundary.
steps: Import μ(k, q) from the same definition the Lean file uses.
Plot μ against k for q = 0 and for any fetched marrow ratio.
Overlay buckling boundaries for the C values the fetched shell formula supports.
Drop any structure without a same-paper modulus.
Report distances to k-star and to the boundary without refitting C.
approaches.decisive_result: One plot of μ(k) and the buckling boundary with every modulus-matched structure marked, and the median |k − k-star| and median distance to the boundary. A type is called buckling-limited only if its median is within 0.10 of the boundary and more than 0.10 from k-star.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than 20 structures have both k and a same-paper modulus, so the plot is an illustration and the approach fails its own sample gate; or the ranking of the two distances flips when C is varied across the values the shell formula allows.
approaches.missing: A specimen-matched modulus for the mammal humeri is not in the Amson table. The curve can still be drawn; most mammal points will lack a buckling coordinate.

problems.title: How do limb bones actually scale with body mass?
problems.question: Across quadrupedal tetrapods, do limb-bone cross-sections scale with body mass at the exponent set by geometric similarity (2/3), elastic similarity (3/4), or stress similarity (1, with posture change compensating), and does the answer depend on clade, posture and bone? Is the scaling of bone safety factor flat?
problems.known_state: Thompson (1917, ch. 2) argues that because bone strength grows as cross-section and weight as volume there is an upper limit to size. McMahon (1973) proposed elastic similarity, with limb-bone diameter scaling as the 3/8 power of length. Biewener (1989) showed that mammals compensate through posture so that bone safety factors stay roughly constant, and Campione and Evans (2012) found a universal relation between body mass and the circumference of the humerus and femur in quadrupeds, with a different scaling for bipeds. Disagreement remains about clade-specific exponents, about phylogenetic correction, and about whether the exponent reflects structural limits or the constraints of locomotion.
acceptance_criteria: A pre-registered phylogenetically corrected regression of limb-bone circumference (or cross-sectional area) on body mass across at least 300 taxa, using the Campione and Evans dataset and an independent compilation, with the three similarity hypotheses and the tolerance on the exponent stated in advance, and clade-by-clade fits.
falsifiers: An exponent interval excluding all three hypotheses, or an exponent that varies significantly across clades after phylogenetic correction, would refute the hypothesis of a single mechanical similarity law.
problems.data_access: Campione and Evans 2012 supplementary data, AnAge and PanTHERIA body masses, and the vendored organisms layer for taxon resolution; independent bone measurements have to be located in published compilations.

related_claims.label: Gravity sets an upper limit on the size of terrestrial animals
Femoral wall thickness follows the bending-moment distribution along the shaft

approaches.title: Pre-registered PGLS of circumference on mass with three fixed exponents
approaches.method: Translate the hypotheses to circumference C (the measure Campione and Evans use): geometric similarity predicts C proportional to M^(1/3), elastic similarity M^(3/8), stress similarity with constant posture M^(1/2) (area proportional to M). Combine the Campione and Evans 2012 supplementary data with an independent compilation (e.g. Alexander et al. 1979 and further published tables found by a pre-registered search) to reach at least 300 quadrupedal taxa, resolve names through the organisms layer and match to a time-calibrated phylogeny (Upham et al. 2019 for mammals; a published composite tree for reptiles and amniotes stated in advance). Fit PGLS with Pagel's lambda estimated by ML (phylolm), separately for humerus, femur and combined circumference, and report both OLS-type and standardized major axis slopes, because the choice changes the exponent and is a known source of disagreement. A hypothesis is accepted if its exponent lies inside the 95% CI and the CI half-width is at most 0.02; the three values differ by 0.042 and 0.125, so the tolerance must be tighter than half the smallest gap.
steps: Download Campione and Evans 2012 additional files; record the exact file and checksum.
Pre-register hypotheses, regression type, tree source, lambda handling, tolerance 0.02 and the clade partition.
Assemble the independent compilation and run a pre-specified duplicate check against Campione and Evans taxa.
Fit PGLS globally and per bone; bootstrap over 100 posterior trees to propagate tree uncertainty.
Report which hypotheses lie in each CI; also refit on the independent compilation alone as a replication.
approaches.decisive_result: Global phylogenetic exponent of C on M with 95% CI of half-width at most 0.02, stating which of 1/3, 3/8, 1/2 it includes, replicated on the independent compilation.
approaches.failure_signature: CI too wide to separate 1/3 from 3/8 (fewer usable taxa than expected), or the exponent differing between the two compilations by more than the CI, indicating measurement or mass-estimation inconsistency.
approaches.missing: An independent compilation large enough to replicate at 300 taxa may need several sources; reptile phylogeny choice adds uncertainty.

approaches.title: Clade and posture heterogeneity of exponents by phylogenetic ANCOVA
approaches.method: The falsifier is clade-dependent exponents. On the dataset of approach 1, fit phylogenetic ANCOVA models with clade-specific slopes (Mammalia orders with at least 15 species, squamates, testudines, crocodylians) and a posture covariate coded in advance (sprawling, semi-erect, erect; cursorial versus not), and compare a single-slope model against clade-slope and posture-slope models by AICc and likelihood ratio, with tree uncertainty propagated over posterior trees. Biewener's posture hypothesis predicts that once posture is in the model, residual clade slopes are not needed; a single mechanical law predicts the single-slope model wins outright.
steps: Pre-register clade partition, posture coding (from literature, coded blind to bone data), minimum clade size and model set.
Fit single, clade-slope, posture-slope and clade-plus-posture models (phylolm, or MCMCglmm with tree as random effect).
Report per-clade exponents with CIs against the three hypotheses.
Check robustness to removing the largest-bodied taxa (elephants, rhinoceroses) and to SMA versus OLS.
approaches.decisive_result: Delta AICc and LR test of the single-slope model versus clade-slope and posture-slope models, with per-clade exponent CIs.
approaches.failure_signature: Clade sample sizes too small to estimate slopes with CI half-width below 0.05, making heterogeneity undetectable rather than absent.

approaches.title: Lean derivation of similarity exponents and the posture-compensation identity
approaches.method: Formalize the three hypotheses as power-law assumptions and derive the exponents, extending Magnitude.lean (which already proves the strength/weight argument for thompson1917-ch02-03). Geometric similarity: all lengths proportional to M^(1/3), so area M^(2/3). Elastic similarity (McMahon): diameter d proportional to l^(3/2) and M proportional to l d^2, so d proportional to M^(3/8), area M^(3/4), length M^(1/4). Stress similarity with posture: peak bone stress sigma proportional to M / (A times EMA) up to a bone-geometry factor; if A proportional to M^a and EMA proportional to M^e then sigma proportional to M^(1 - a - e), so constant stress (flat safety factor if strength is size-independent) requires a + e = 1. Prove these as theorems over real exponents. Then plug in the published estimates of a (from approach 1) and of e (Biewener 1989) to state the implied stress exponent with propagated uncertainty, giving a numerical test of whether the safety factor is flat.
steps: Define power-law scaling relations as functions f(M) = c M^p with Real.rpow and prove the composition lemmas.
Prove the three exponent derivations and the stress identity sigma exponent = 1 - a - e.
Prove that a + e = 1 is necessary and sufficient for size-independent stress under the stated model.
Record in lean/reports; compute 1 - a - e with delta-method or bootstrap CIs using approach 1's a and Biewener's e, labelled as a data-dependent corollary, not a theorem.
approaches.decisive_result: Compiled Lean module with no sorry for the derivations and the identity, plus the stress-exponent estimate with 95% CI and whether it includes 0.
approaches.failure_signature: The data step: if EMA estimates exist for too few species to give a CI on e narrower than 0.1, the safety-factor question stays open even though the formal part completes.
approaches.missing: Effective mechanical advantage data across many species are limited to a few published compilations.

approaches.title: Preregistered phylogenetic model contest for limb-bone scaling
approaches.method: Reanalyse the Campione and Evans quadruped measurements and an independently curated compilation, resolving taxa through the organisms layer. For circumference, cross-sectional area and section modulus separately, fit phylogenetic generalized least squares and multilevel models with bone, clade and posture interactions. Compare point hypotheses for area exponents 2/3, 3/4 and 1 using a predeclared equivalence margin of 0.04, while estimating phylogenetic uncertainty over a tree ensemble rather than one tree.
steps: Vendor measurements, body masses, posture classes and a dated tree ensemble with provenance.
Freeze exclusion, log transformation, equivalence margin and outlier rules.
Fit pooled and clade-by-bone models and test heterogeneity before selecting a universal exponent.
Validate on the independent compilation and report prediction intervals, not only coefficients.
approaches.decisive_result: A universal law is accepted only if the pooled exponent is within 0.04 of one candidate, the 95% interval excludes the other two margins, clade standard deviation is below 0.04, and the independent dataset reproduces that classification; otherwise universality is rejected.
approaches.failure_signature: Failure to reproduce the exponent independently, clade heterogeneity at least 0.04, or intervals overlapping multiple hypotheses defeats a single similarity law.
approaches.missing: An independent compilation with comparable posture metadata must be located; circumference alone does not identify safety factor.

approaches.title: Mechanistic safety-factor scaling with posture compensation
approaches.method: For a mammal subset with force-plate or published peak ground-reaction forces, combine body mass, limb effective mechanical advantage, bone length and CT-derived section modulus to estimate peak bending plus axial stress and safety factor. Fit two causal models: geometry-only similarity and posture-compensated stress similarity. Use measurement-error propagation and leave-clade-out prediction; the target is whether nearly flat safety factors arise only after posture is included.
steps: Scout at least 40 species with matchable gait force, posture and limb geometry records.
Pre-register load decomposition, muscle-force bounds and admissible taxonomic matching.
Estimate stress and safety-factor allometry with and without posture.
Test predictions in a held-out clade and conduct sensitivity analysis over material strength.
approaches.decisive_result: Posture compensation is supported if the mass slope of log safety factor has absolute value below 0.05 only in the posture model, and that model lowers held-out stress RMSE by at least 20% relative to geometry-only similarity.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than 40 matched species, a non-flat safety-factor slope after posture, or no predictive gain means the approach fails to explain scaling by mechanical similarity.
approaches.missing: The necessary force, posture, CT geometry and material-strength measurements are not known to coexist publicly for 40 species.

approaches.title: Phylogenetic slopes of limb-bone size on body mass
approaches.method: Two open tables, analysed separately and then counted together. Campione and Evans, as redistributed in the MASSTIMATE package data frame extants, give body mass and humeral and femoral circumference for 245 extant tetrapods. Use only those extant rows. Dinosaur rows in the paper's supplement are excluded, because their masses are estimated from the limb bones. Amson and Bibi give body mass and humeral MeanArea for 152 mammal species, with a deposited timetree. The model is log(y) = α + β log(mass) + error, fitted by phylogenetic generalised least squares with Pagel's λ: covariance σ² (λ V + (1 − λ) I), λ by maximum likelihood. For circumference the three hypotheses are β = 1/3 (geometric), 3/8 (elastic) and 1/2 (stress). For cross-sectional area they are β = 2/3, 3/4 and 1. Campione circumferences also yield a circular-section area proxy C² / (4π), labelled as a proxy. A hypothesis is compatible if the 95 percent interval of β contains it, and it is the unique winner if it is the only compatible one. Clade fits use each order with at least 15 species. The exponent varies across clades if at least two such orders have intervals that exclude the pooled estimate. Mammal trees come from the Upham, Esselstyn and Jetz posterior; names are resolved through the organisms layer to GBIF. Reptiles in Campione are fitted by ordinary least squares unless a fetched tree file covers them, and that split is reported. The safety-factor claim is not measured here: constant stress under geometric posture is the area exponent 1, and no strain gauge data are in these tables. The problem asks for 300 taxa. The decisive count is the number of unique species across the two tables after name resolution. If that count is under 300, the fits are still reported and the coverage clause fails.
steps: Pre-register the three exponents, the compatibility rule and the dinosaur exclusion before fitting.
Load MASSTIMATE extants and the Amson humerus table; resolve names to GBIF.
Build the mammal covariance from the Upham trees and the Amson timetree for that table.
Fit PGLS for humerus and femur, pooled and by order with n ≥ 15.
Report which hypotheses are compatible, and the unique-species count against 300.
approaches.decisive_result: The PGLS slope and 95 percent interval for each bone and each table, the list of compatible hypotheses, the order-level slopes, and the unique-species count. A single similarity law is supported only if one hypothesis is the unique winner in both tables and no two large orders exclude the pooled estimate. The 300-taxon bar is met only if the deduplicated union reaches 300.
approaches.failure_signature: Tree mismatch drops more than half the species; every interval is wider than 0.25 so no hypothesis is excluded; the two tables pick different unique winners; or the unique-species count stays under 300.
approaches.missing: A reptile phylogeny file was not verified in the Campione supplement. In vivo bone strain and effective mechanical advantage are not in either table, so safety-factor flatness is not measured. The extant Campione table has 245 species, under the problem's 300 until the union is counted.

approaches.title: Lean derivation of the three similarity exponents
approaches.method: The data test needs its targets to be theorems. From the scaling assumptions, prove in Lean, next to the existing strength-to-weight lemmas in ThompsonLaws.Magnitude: geometric similarity (every length proportional to mass to the 1/3) implies cross-sectional area proportional to mass to the 2/3 and circumference to the 1/3; elastic similarity as McMahon stated it (diameter proportional to mass to the 3/8, length to the 1/4) implies area proportional to mass to the 3/4; stress similarity (force proportional to mass and stress equal to force over area held constant) implies area proportional to mass to the 1 and circumference to the 1/2. Prove the three area exponents are distinct. Also prove the posture lemma in elementary form: if effective mechanical advantage scales as mass to the γ, constant bone stress is compatible with area proportional to mass to the 1 − γ. No organism is asserted to follow any of these.
steps: State the three assumption sets as Lean hypotheses.
Prove the area and circumference exponents.
Prove the exponents are pairwise distinct.
Prove the effective-mechanical-advantage correction 1 − γ.
Compile with no sorry and point the data test at these constants.
approaches.decisive_result: Sorry-free theorems giving area exponents 2/3, 3/4 and 1, circumference exponents 1/3, 3/8 and 1/2, and the posture correction 1 − γ.
approaches.failure_signature: One classical exponent does not follow from the assumptions as formalised. That hypothesis is then withdrawn from the data test rather than forced.

approaches.title: Does the area-mass exponent differ by lifestyle?
approaches.method: The problem asks whether the exponent depends on posture. These tables do not contain effective mechanical advantage. Amson and Bibi do code lifestyle (aerial, terrestrial, aquatic, subterranean) and deposit a timetree. Fit log(MeanArea) = α_L + β_L log(mass) by PGLS inside each lifestyle with at least 20 species, using their tree. Posture dependence, in this proxy, is supported if at least one pair of lifestyles has slope estimates differing by more than 0.08 (the gap between 2/3 and 3/4) and non-overlapping 95 percent intervals. Lifestyle is not joint posture, and the write-up says so. This does not test safety-factor flatness.
steps: Pre-register the 0.08 gap and the minimum of 20 species before fitting.
Split the humerus table by the deposited lifestyle codes.
Fit one PGLS slope per lifestyle on the deposited timetree.
Compare intervals pairwise.
State that the covariate is lifestyle, not effective mechanical advantage.
approaches.decisive_result: Four lifestyle slopes with intervals. Dependence is accepted only if some pair differs by more than 0.08 with disjoint intervals. Otherwise the deposited lifestyle codes do not identify a different similarity law.
approaches.failure_signature: Every lifestyle with at least 20 species has an interval that overlaps all three of 2/3, 3/4 and 1, or a lifestyle class falls under 20 species so the comparison cannot be made.
approaches.missing: Effective mechanical advantage and in vivo strain are not in this file, so the safety-factor claim stays open.

problems.title: Do real hygromorphs follow bilayer curvature and diffusive response-time scaling?
problems.question: For humidity-driven plant structures (pine cone scales, wheat awns, seed pods) and for fabricated bilayers, does curvature follow the Timoshenko bilayer prediction from the measured swelling mismatch and layer stiffnesses, and does the response time scale as thickness squared over the water diffusivity? How large are the deviations from fibre orientation, graded properties and viscoelasticity?
problems.known_state: Timoshenko (1925) gave the bilayer curvature formula for thermal mismatch, and Reyssat and Mahadevan (2009) apply it to hygromorphs, with response time set by diffusion through the thickness. Dawson, Vincent and Rocca (1997) showed that pine cone scales open by differential swelling of two tissue layers, and Armon et al. (2011) analysed the geometry of chiral seed pods. The repo carries machine-checked statements of the bilayer curvature, the response time and the antisymmetric twist in `claim-sources/plant-hygromorph-mechanics` (Lean modules in the Thompson Lake project). What is missing is a systematic comparison of measured curvature and response time against these predictions across species and across fabricated bilayers.
acceptance_criteria: A pre-registered test on at least 20 plant hygromorph specimens from at least five species, or on printed bilayers of at least three thicknesses and two swelling mismatches, in which curvature and response time are predicted from independently measured moduli, swelling strains and diffusivity and the pass tolerance is fixed in advance.
falsifiers: If measured curvature differs from the Timoshenko prediction by more than the stated tolerance in most specimens, or if response time does not scale with thickness squared, the model is refuted for those structures.
problems.data_access: Published curvature and response-time data from Reyssat and Mahadevan 2009, Dawson et al. 1997 and Armon et al. 2011; fabricated bilayers need a printer and a humidity chamber, which the swarm lacks.

related_claims.label: Annular, longitudinal and spiral wall thickenings of plant cells are cylinder geodetics

approaches.title: Literature-extracted test of curvature and h^2/D response time across species
approaches.method: Extend the repo's pre-registered pine-cone curvature test to the full acceptance criterion using published data only. For each specimen or specimen class in pine cone scales (Reyssat and Mahadevan 2009; Quan et al. 2021; Eger et al. 2022; Dawson et al. 1997), wheat awns (Elbaum et al. 2007), chiral seed pods (Armon et al. 2011) and fabricated bilayers (paper-polymer in Reyssat and Mahadevan; Erb et al. 2013; Gladman et al. 2016; Le Duigou and Castro 2016), extract layer thicknesses, moduli, free swelling strains, diffusivity or permeability, measured curvature change and response time. Predict curvature with the Lean-checked Timoshenko formula (bilayerCurvature_ofEquilibrium) and response time with tau = h^2/D (diffusiveTime_scale). Pass: |log(kappa_measured/kappa_pred)| <= log 1.5 in most specimens; response time slope on log h equals 2 within plus or minus 0.4 among fabricated bilayers of at least three thicknesses.
steps: Pre-register tolerances, extraction rules (only inputs measured independently of the curvature itself; no back-fitted swelling strains) and the specimen count required (20 specimens, five species, or the fabricated-bilayer alternative).
Extract from text, tables and digitized figures (with digitization error recorded).
Compute predictions and residuals; report per species.
Fit log tau on log h for fabricated series with a mixed model by study; report slope and CI.
Classify deviations by suspected cause (fibre angle, gradient, viscoelasticity) for approach 2.
approaches.decisive_result: Per-specimen curvature ratio distribution and response-time exponent with CI, against the pre-registered tolerances.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than 20 specimens with all inputs independently measured (most papers fit swelling strain from curvature, which is circular); response time series with fewer than three thicknesses.
approaches.missing: Independent per-specimen moduli, swelling strains and diffusivity are rarely reported together; no humidity chamber or printer to measure new specimens.

approaches.title: FE correction factors for fibre angle, gradients and poroelastic lag
approaches.method: Quantify, before looking at data, how far real hygromorph features push curvature and response time from the Timoshenko and h^2/D predictions. Run FEniCSx models of strips with (a) misaligned swelling direction at angle phi (reducing bending and adding twist, consistent with the Lean-checked antisymmetric-twist theorems), (b) continuously graded modulus and eigenstrain through the thickness, (c) imperfect bonding via a compliant interlayer, (d) poroelastic coupling with layer-specific diffusivities, and (e) linear viscoelastic relaxation. Produce dimensionless correction maps kappa_FE/kappa_Timoshenko and tau_FE/(h^2/D) over the parameter ranges reported for pine cones, awns and printed bilayers. These maps convert approach 1 from a pass/fail of the ideal model into a test of whether measured deviations are explained by measured structure.
steps: Verify the FE code against the Timoshenko formula (error below 1% for slender, perfectly bonded, uniform layers) and against the first diffusion mode decay rate pi^2 D/h^2.
Sweep each departure separately over literature ranges, then in pairs.
Publish correction tables and the parameter region where Timoshenko is within 10%.
Pre-register their use as the 'structure-corrected' model in approach 1.
approaches.decisive_result: Correction maps with the boundary of the 10% validity region of the ideal model for each departure, checked for mesh convergence.
approaches.failure_signature: Corrections that depend on unmeasured parameters (e.g. interlayer compliance) so strongly that any measured curvature can be fitted, making the corrected model unfalsifiable.

approaches.title: Lean: graded-beam curvature integral reducing to Timoshenko
approaches.method: Generalize the existing Hygromorphs.lean results from two uniform layers to arbitrary through-thickness profiles E(z) and eigenstrain eps(z). With moments A = integral E, B = integral E z, D = integral E z^2, P = integral E eps, Q = integral E z eps over the thickness, force and moment balance give curvature kappa = (A Q - B P)/(A D - B^2). Prove this from equilibrium for integrable profiles (interval integrals in Mathlib), prove A D - B^2 > 0 for positive non-constant-free E (Cauchy-Schwarz), and prove it reduces to the existing bilayerCurvature for piecewise-constant two-layer profiles. Also prove that for a two-layer strip with diffusivities D1 and D2 the slowest diffusion time lies between h^2/(pi^2 D_max) and h^2/(pi^2 D_min) for the stated separable model, or state the bound as a conditional theorem if the spectral argument exceeds current Mathlib.
steps: Define the moment integrals with intervalIntegral and state equilibrium.
Prove the curvature formula and the positivity of the denominator.
Prove the reduction to bilayerCurvature for two-layer step profiles.
Attempt the diffusion-time bracket; if not feasible, record precisely what Mathlib lacks.
Update the Hygromorphs report.
approaches.decisive_result: Compiled Lean theorems for the graded curvature formula and its reduction to Timoshenko, with no sorry.
approaches.failure_signature: Integration lemmas for piecewise-constant functions too cumbersome to close the reduction; diffusion bracket left unproved (partial completion).
approaches.missing: The diffusion-time bracket for heterogeneous layers needs spectral theory of Sturm-Liouville operators that Mathlib may not provide.

approaches.title: Independent-parameter audit of plant bilayer predictions
approaches.method: Extract specimen-level or reconstructable measurements for at least 20 hygromorphs from five species: layer thicknesses, orthotropic moduli, free swelling strains, moisture diffusivity, curvature-time traces and humidity step. Predict equilibrium curvature with the Timoshenko bilayer formula and response time with the first diffusion eigenmode without fitting either outcome. Pre-register error tolerances, digitization uncertainty and a graded orthotropic alternative, then use leave-species-out prediction to prevent species-specific calibration.
steps: Scout papers and supplements for jointly reported inputs and outcomes.
Dual-digitize figures and reject records lacking independently measured inputs.
Compute parameter-free bilayer predictions and uncertainty intervals.
Compare simple, orthotropic and viscoelastic models by leave-species-out predictive error.
approaches.decisive_result: The simple scaling passes if at least 16 of 20 equilibrium curvatures are within 25% of prediction and the fitted log response-time versus log thickness slope is within 0.25 of 2 with a 95% interval; otherwise report which extension achieves at least a 20% held-out error reduction.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than 20 jointly parameterized specimens, systematic curvature error above 25%, or a response-time slope interval excluding 2 by more than 0.25 refutes the simple model for the assembled species.
approaches.missing: Published papers may not expose enough specimen-level combinations of moduli, swelling mismatch, diffusivity and time courses to reach 20 records.

approaches.title: Identifiability map for bilayer, graded and viscoelastic hygromorphs
approaches.method: Implement finite-element models for a sharp isotropic bilayer, an orthotropic bilayer, a continuous stiffness/swelling gradient and a viscoelastic bilayer. Sweep thickness ratio, modulus ratio, fibre angle, Biot number and relaxation-to-diffusion time ratio, then create synthetic curvature-time traces with realistic noise. Fit all four models blind to determine when curvature and response time can distinguish the simple law from its extensions and which additional observable is required when they cannot.
steps: Verify the simple solver against the existing bilayer curvature and diffusion limits.
Run a Latin-hypercube sweep with mesh and time-step convergence.
Perform blinded model recovery from synthetic traces.
Publish a decision map and minimal measurement design for future specimens.
approaches.decisive_result: The approach succeeds with a reproducible map identifying parameter regions where the true model is recovered with at least 90% accuracy and a ranked extra observable, such as through-thickness strain or relaxation after humidity reversal, for non-identifiable regions.
approaches.failure_signature: Failure to recover even the generating model under low noise, or universal non-identifiability across the sweep, shows curvature-time data cannot test the proposed deviations.
approaches.missing: The result designs and validates a discriminator but does not supply new biological measurements.

approaches.title: Published curvature and response time against the bilayer laws
approaches.method: The curvature formula and the diffusive time τ = h² / D are already theorems in ThompsonLaws.Hygromorphs (bilayerCurvature_ofEquilibrium, diffusiveTime_scale). The missing piece is the comparison with measurements. Extract, from tables when they exist and from figures only when they do not, every specimen that reports layer thicknesses, moduli and a swelling strain measured independently of the curvature, plus the measured curvature change. Response-time rows need thickness and a time constant after a humidity step. Sources to extract, in this order: Quan, Pirosa, Yang, Ritchie and Meyers 2021 (open access pine-cone scales), Reyssat and Mahadevan 2009 (pine scales and paper-polymer bilayers), Dawson, Vincent and Rocca 1997, Elbaum and colleagues 2007 on wheat awns, and Armon, Efrati, Kupferman and Sharon 2011 on chiral pods. Predicted curvature uses the Lean formula. Pass, pre-registered: median |κ_measured − κ_predicted| / |κ_predicted| ≤ 0.50, the sign of curvature correct in at least 90 percent of specimens, and the ordinary-least-squares slope of log(τ) on log(h) has a 95 percent interval that contains 2 and excludes 1 and 3. Swelling strains fitted from the curvature itself are forbidden. The problem's coverage bar is at least 20 specimens from five species, or fabricated bilayers at three thicknesses and two swelling mismatches. The Reyssat paper-polymer series is the fabricated arm and does not require the swarm to print.
steps: Pre-register the 0.50 relative-error band, the sign rule and the slope exclusions before extracting numbers.
Pull independently measured inputs from the open papers; mark every figure-digitised point.
Reject rows whose swelling strain was fitted from curvature.
Compute Timoshenko curvature and the log-log time slope.
Score coverage against 20 specimens and five species, and against the fabricated-bilayer alternative.
approaches.decisive_result: The per-specimen relative curvature error and the response-time slope with its interval, on a sample that meets one of the two coverage bars. The model passes only if the median relative error is ≤ 0.50, the sign is right in ≥ 90 percent of rows, and the time-slope interval contains 2 and excludes 1 and 3.
approaches.failure_signature: The open record does not reach 20 specimens from five species or the fabricated thickness series; most papers only back-calculate swelling from curvature; the median relative error exceeds 0.50; or the time-slope interval misses 2 or includes 1 or 3.
approaches.missing: No humidity chamber and no printer, so no new specimens. Several of the papers expose only figures, and a scripted fetch of the Royal Society and Science landing pages returned 403, so some tables may be unreachable.

approaches.title: Size of curvature and time errors when the assumptions fail
approaches.method: Quantify the deviations the problem asks about, as a model bound rather than a plant measurement. Start from the two-layer Euler-Bernoulli equilibrium already proved in Lean and check that a numerical beam recovers κ = (3/2) Δε / h when thicknesses and moduli are equal, to within 1 percent. Then solve three extensions the theorems do not cover: a linear through-thickness modulus gradient, a standard-linear-solid viscoelastic branch in the active layer, and a fibre angle that adds the shear mismatch already defined for the antisymmetric-twist claim. On a grid of modulus ratio from 0.1 to 10, gradient strength, viscosity ratio and fibre angle from 0 to 45 degrees, record κ divided by the Timoshenko value and the apparent exponent d log τ / d log h.
steps: Verify the numerical beam against bilayerCurvature_symmetric to 1 percent.
Add the modulus gradient, the viscoelastic branch and the fibre angle one at a time.
Sweep the pre-registered grid.
Tabulate relative curvature error and the apparent time exponent.
Mark cells where the absolute relative curvature error exceeds 0.50 or the time exponent leaves [1.5, 2.5].
approaches.decisive_result: The grid of κ / κ_Timoshenko and of the apparent time exponent. Deviations are large, by the pre-registered rule, where the absolute relative curvature error exceeds 0.50 or the time exponent leaves [1.5, 2.5]. The symmetric-case check must pass or the grid is void.
approaches.failure_signature: The solver misses the Lean symmetric curvature by more than 1 percent, or the error changes sign when the mesh is refined by two, so the deviation table is a discretisation artefact.

approaches.title: Lean bound on curvature error under a modulus perturbation
approaches.method: The equilibrium theorem already gives κ as a smooth function of the two moduli. Prove a perturbation bound: if both moduli are multiplied by factors within (1 − ε, 1 + ε) with ε < 1/2 and the thicknesses stay positive, the relative change in curvature is at most an explicit f(ε) derived from the formula, not a fitted constant. The bound covers modulus error only. Fibre angle, grading and viscosity are outside it, and the theorem says so. This is the piece of the deviation question that is an inequality rather than a sweep.
steps: Treat bilayerCurvature as a function of the two moduli.
Differentiate it under the existing positivity hypotheses.
Prove a concrete relative-error inequality for ε < 1/2.
Compile with no sorry.
approaches.decisive_result: A sorry-free theorem giving an explicit f such that the relative curvature change is ≤ f(ε) whenever both moduli move by at most the factor 1 + ε, ε < 1/2.
approaches.failure_signature: The bound does not close without assuming the curvature formula rather than the equilibrium hypotheses, or sorry remains. Fibre angle and viscosity are not a failure; they are out of scope and must not be smuggled into the statement.

approaches.title: Operator protocol for bilayers at three thicknesses
approaches.method: The acceptance criterion allows printed bilayers of at least three thicknesses and two swelling mismatches instead of 20 plant specimens. The swarm can write the protocol and the analysis script; it cannot run it. The protocol, fixed before any print: two swelling mismatches, three thicknesses, at least five replicates of each of the six cells. Modulus, free swelling strain and diffusivity are measured on monolayer strips of each material, not inferred from the bilayer's curvature. Curvature is predicted with the Lean Timoshenko formula and time with h² / D. Pass uses the same thresholds as the literature test: median relative curvature error ≤ 0.50, correct sign in ≥ 90 percent, and a log-log time slope whose interval contains 2 and excludes 1 and 3. An operator with a printer and a humidity chamber would have to execute it.
steps: Publish the protocol with the six-cell design and the pass thresholds.
Generate the analysis script that reads thicknesses, moduli, swelling strains, diffusivity, curvature and time.
Stop. Do not invent measurements.
If an operator later deposits a file, run the script unchanged.
approaches.decisive_result: Measured curvature and response time on the six-cell design, scored with the pre-registered thresholds. The script alone is not the result.
approaches.failure_signature: No operator runs the prints, which is the expected outcome, or the prints are run but the median relative error exceeds 0.50 or the time slope misses 2.
approaches.missing: A printer, a humidity chamber and an operator. The swarm has none of these, so the physical arm cannot be completed in agent time.

problems.title: How much of biomineral form is physical, and how much is cell-controlled?
problems.question: For single-cell skeletons (radiolarian lattices, foraminiferal chambers, sponge spicules, coccoliths) and sea urchin spicules, which geometric features of the mineral are predicted by surface-tension and packing physics alone, and which require a matrix template or cellular control? Does the same geometry appear when different minerals are laid down on the same vesicle pattern?
problems.known_state: Thompson (1917, ch. 9) holds that skeletal elements the size of a cell are shaped by molecular forces such as surface tension, and that the hexagonal lattice shells of Radiolaria, Acantharia and Clathrulina are equally regular in silica, strontium sulphate and an organic substance (ch. 9-15). Modern work shows that many biominerals form through a transient amorphous precursor that is moulded and then crystallizes (Politi et al. 2004; Weiner and Addadi 2011), which supports cellular control of shape and of polymorph, but does not directly test the physical-forces claims. No quantitative comparison of the predicted foam-packing geometry against measured lattice geometry across taxa exists.
acceptance_criteria: A pre-registered comparison of mesh geometry (polygon-side distribution, vertex angles, spacing) in at least 30 radiolarian, acantharian and related lattice shells from open image archives against the foam-packing prediction and against a null of random Voronoi tessellation, with the match criterion stated in advance.
falsifiers: If measured lattices are no closer to the foam-packing prediction than to a random Voronoi null, Thompson's physical-forces explanation is refuted for these taxa.
If mineral identity predicts geometry once vesicle pattern is fixed, the claim of mineral-independence is refuted.
problems.data_access: Open radiolarian and foraminiferal plates (Haeckel's Challenger monographs and modern SEM archives), micrographs in the repo's cell-geometry project, and published SEM of sea urchin spicules; the availability of paired mineral and vesicle data is uncertain and has to be scouted.

related_claims.label: Cell-sized skeletal elements are shaped by molecular forces, large ones by mechanics
Hexagonal lattice shells form as silica collects in grooves between surface vesicles
Lattice-shell form is independent of the material, being moulded on vesicles

approaches.title: Mesh statistics of radiolarian lattice shells against foam and two Voronoi nulls
approaches.method: Reuse the cell-geometry pipeline (Cellpose segmentation, junction-angle and neighbour-count analysis, synthetic controls) on images of latticed radiolarian shells. Primary data must be micrographs (SEM or light), because Haeckel's plates are idealized drawings; use them only as a secondary, explicitly flagged set. Measure in the central region of each shell where foreshortening is below 10% (or correct projection on a fitted sphere): fraction of trivalent vertices, vertex-angle SD around 120 degrees, polygon-side distribution and its second moment mu2, Lewis's law slope (pore area versus sides) and Aboav-Weaire. Compare to three references fixed in advance: a relaxed foam (Plateau borders, simulated by vertex model at matched polydispersity), a Poisson-Voronoi null, and a hard-core (equal-sized random packing) Voronoi null. The hard-core null is essential: equal vesicle packing alone yields many hexagons without surface tension, so only vertex angles and mu2 at matched polydispersity can separate surface-tension moulding from packing. Euler's relation forces mean sides near 6 on any trivalent net, so mean side number is excluded as evidence (the lesson of the repo's ch07-10 result).
steps: Scout image sources with licences: mikrotax radiolaria pages, the Tetard et al. 2020 radiolarian image workflow data, Wikimedia Commons, and open-access SEM figures; record species, mineral and magnification.

Pre-register: at least 30 shells, the central-region rule, the metrics, the nulls, and the match criterion (vertex-angle SD and mu2 closer to the foam reference than to both Voronoi nulls, by bootstrap over shells).
Segment pores (Cellpose via Nebius, or classical watershed if Cellpose fails on lattice images; compare both).
Simulate the three references at each shell's measured pore-size polydispersity.
Report per shell and pooled; publish as a claim test on thompson1917-ch09-14.
approaches.decisive_result: For at least 30 micrograph-imaged shells, vertex-angle SD and mu2 significantly closer to the matched foam reference than to both Poisson and hard-core Voronoi nulls (or not), with segmentation error bounded by synthetic-lattice calibration.
approaches.failure_signature: Segmentation of 3D lattice shells in 2D images too unreliable (calibration error larger than the foam-versus-hard-core gap), or fewer than 30 licensed micrographs.
approaches.missing: A licensed set of high-resolution micrographs of latticed shells; Cellpose was trained on cells, not mineral lattices, so segmentation may need a custom method.

approaches.title: Equivalence test of lattice regularity across silica, SrSO4 and organic shells
approaches.method: Test the mineral-independence claim (thompson1917-ch09-15) directly: compare mesh-regularity metrics from approach 1 (vertex-angle SD, mu2, hexagon fraction at matched polydispersity) between silica lattice shells (Spumellaria), strontium sulphate lattice shells (Acantharia with latticed shells) and the organic lattice of Clathrulina. Use two one-sided tests (TOST) with an equivalence margin fixed in advance from a pilot on synthetic lattices (the margin is set to half the difference in each metric between the matched foam reference and the hard-core Voronoi null of approach 1, so 'equivalent' means closer than the physics-versus-packing distinction can resolve), with mixed models by taxon. Equivalence supports mineral-independent moulding; a mineral effect beyond the margin refutes it. The underlying vesicle pattern is not observable in fixed shells, so this tests mineral-independence of the final geometry, not 'given the same vesicle pattern'; that limitation is stated.
steps: Scout images for each mineral group, with at least 10 shells per group; Clathrulina SEM is the likely bottleneck.
Pre-register metrics, margin and the mixed-model TOST.
Run approach 1's pipeline on all shells.
Report equivalence or difference per metric.
approaches.decisive_result: TOST result per metric across the three mineral groups, with at least 10 shells each.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than 10 usable Clathrulina or latticed acantharian images, leaving the comparison underpowered.
approaches.missing: Open micrographs of Acantharia lattice shells and Clathrulina in sufficient number; no culture or microscope to generate them.

approaches.title: Spherical vesicle-foam simulation with Plateau-border deposition
approaches.method: Generate the physical prediction explicitly rather than borrowing planar foam statistics. Simulate a monolayer of N vesicles on a sphere with a 2D vertex model (line tension on edges, area constraint per vesicle, polydispersity parameter s), relax to equilibrium, and deposit mineral along edges (Plateau borders). Vary N and s. Record pore polygon distribution, vertex angles, defect (non-hexagon) positions and their spacing. Two physics checks that are not discriminating, and should be reported as such: on any trivalent spherical net the sum over faces of (6 - n) is exactly 12 (Euler), and mean sides approach 6 as N grows. The discriminating outputs are the vertex-angle distribution, the defect-correlation length (defects in relaxed foams arrange in scars or are spread; in random packings they are uncorrelated) and Lewis-law slope at a given s. Fit s per real shell and test whether a single s reproduces all statistics jointly (posterior predictive check).
steps: Implement a spherical vertex model in Python (or use Surface Evolver if available) and verify against known results for monodisperse 2D foams.
Prove or cite the Euler identity sum (6 - n) = 12 for trivalent spherical nets (a short Lean lemma assuming V - E + F = 2 and trivalence).
Sweep N in 20..500 and s in 0..0.5; build summary-statistic emulators.
Fit s per shell from approach 1 data by approximate Bayesian computation and run joint posterior predictive checks.
approaches.decisive_result: Posterior predictive p-values for the joint statistics of each shell under the fitted foam model; most shells reproduced (p > 0.05) supports the physical explanation, systematic failure in vertex angles or defect correlation refutes it.
approaches.failure_signature: Model statistics insensitive to line tension versus pure packing at realistic N, so no observable can separate them; or approach 1 data unavailable.
approaches.missing: Depends on approach 1's measured shells for the comparison step; the simulation alone is tractable.

approaches.title: Spherical-lattice geometry contest across mineral classes
approaches.method: Assemble at least 30 calibrated, near-orthographic SEM or optical images spanning silica radiolarians, strontium-sulphate acantharians and organic Clathrulina-like lattices, with at least eight specimens per material class. Segment vertices and edges blind to material, correct spherical projection where possible, and measure polygon-side counts, vertex angles, edge-length coefficient of variation and topological defects. Compare a noisy equal-area foam model, a spherical Poisson-Voronoi null and a phylogenetically structured material model using held-out image likelihood.
steps: Scout images with taxon, scale and composition provenance and freeze inclusion criteria.
Validate segmentation against duplicate manual annotations on 20% of images.
Simulate matched-size foam and random-Voronoi nulls on the sphere.
Fit material and phylogenetic effects and perform leave-taxon-out prediction.
approaches.decisive_result: Packing physics is supported for mature geometry if the foam model improves held-out log predictive density over random Voronoi in all three materials and material class explains under 5% additional variance; a material effect above 20% refutes mineral independence.
approaches.failure_signature: No advantage over random Voronoi, segmentation error comparable to model differences, or fewer than eight usable specimens in any material class defeats this comparison.
approaches.missing: The availability and licensing of enough calibrated acantharian and organic-lattice SEM images are uncertain; mature images cannot establish the developmental vesicle mechanism.

approaches.title: Morphology fingerprints of templating versus self-organization
approaches.method: Generate preregistered morphology fingerprints for three mechanisms on a curved surface: equal-area vesicle packing with deposition in interfaces, Cahn-Hilliard phase separation with mineral precipitation, and an explicit cell-template field with controlled spatial correlations. Match only area fraction and mean spacing, then compare higher-order observables that were not fitted: defect charge versus curvature, three-point correlations, edge-width distribution and concentric-layer registration. Apply the frozen classifier to the image set from the geometry test.
steps: Implement and convergence-test all three mechanism classes on identical spherical meshes.
Generate a balanced simulation library over nuisance parameters.
Train a classifier on simulations using only preregistered higher-order observables.
Run simulation-based calibration and then classify biological images with an abstention threshold.
approaches.decisive_result: A bounded mechanism is distinguished if synthetic held-out accuracy exceeds 90% and at least 70% of biological images receive posterior probability above 0.8 for one class; otherwise the tested morphology is non-identifying.
approaches.failure_signature: Synthetic mechanisms overlap after matching area fraction and spacing, classifier calibration fails, or biological images mostly trigger abstention, showing geometry alone cannot separate control modes.
approaches.missing: This can reject morphological sufficiency but cannot prove cellular control without developmental imaging or perturbation data.

approaches.title: Lattice angles against a foam and a Poisson-Voronoi null
approaches.method: Segment at least 30 spherical lattice shells from Haeckel's Challenger plates (public domain) and from mikrotax pages that actually display a drawing or photograph. Plates 1 to 50 are Spumellaria (silica) and plates 129 to 140 are Acantharia (strontium sulphate); only lattice shells are measured, not spicular skeletons. Record the polygon side-count histogram and the interior angles at each vertex. Two nulls are generated by the swarm, not taken from a remembered table: a Poisson-Voronoi tessellation on the sphere with the same cell count, and a Lloyd (centroidal Voronoi) relaxation used as the foam proxy, whose vertices approach 120 degree meetings. The statistics are the circular standard deviation of vertex angles about 120 degrees, and the total-variation distance between side-count histograms. A shell supports the foam prediction if it is closer to the Lloyd null than to the Poisson-Voronoi null on both statistics. Pass is a pre-registered majority of at least 70 percent of the 30 shells. Drawings and photographs are scored separately; a foam match that appears only in drawings does not confirm the biological claim. Mineral independence, for thompson1917-ch09-15, is a permutation test of angle scatter between silica and strontium-sulphate lattice shells, and it is run only if at least ten lattice shells exist in each class. It fails if the permutation p is under 0.01 and the median angle scatter differs by more than 5 degrees. The same angle pipeline on nannotax coccoliths is the cellular-control contrast: they are not predicted to be foams, and the test only asks which null they are closer to. Mature shells do not show the vesicle grooves of thompson1917-ch09-14.
steps: Pre-register the 70 percent majority, the 10-shell mineral gate and the drawing-versus-photograph split.
Download Haeckel plates and mikrotax images that display a lattice; skip pages without an image.
Segment sides and vertex angles for at least 30 shells.
Generate Poisson-Voronoi and Lloyd nulls matched in cell count.
Score foam versus Voronoi, then the mineral split, then the coccolith contrast.
approaches.decisive_result: Side-count and angle-scatter distances for at least 30 shells, a foam majority only if at least 70 percent are closer to the Lloyd null on both statistics in the photograph subset as well as the drawings, and a mineral comparison only if both classes have at least ten lattice shells.
approaches.failure_signature: Shells are no closer to the Lloyd foam than to Poisson-Voronoi; the foam match is confined to drawings; fewer than ten lattice shells exist for one mineral; or the mineral classes differ by more than 5 degrees at permutation p < 0.01, which refutes mineral independence.
approaches.missing: Paired vesicle and mineral maps of growing shells are not in these archives, so the groove mechanism is untested. A modern image set of organic Clathrulina lattices was not verified. Mikrotax radiolaria is a developing catalogue and may lack thirty usable photographs.

approaches.title: Twelve pentagons are a topological count
approaches.method: A spherical lattice of hexagons and pentagons with three edges at every vertex has exactly twelve pentagons, by Euler's formula. Prove it in Lean from the handshaking hypotheses the statement names: V − E + F = 2, 2E = 3V, and 2E = 5P + 6H with F = P + H, hence P = 12. The count does not depend on a material parameter. That is the mineral-independence of this one integer, for thompson1917-ch09-15, and it does not say the angles are 120 degrees. Applicability is an empirical gate owned by the image test: if more than 20 percent of segmented vertices have degree other than 3, the hypothesis is not the biological case. The proof itself does not wait on that count.
steps: State the handshaking hypotheses.
Prove P = 12.
Prove the count is unchanged if a material parameter is added to the context and never used.
Compile with no sorry.
approaches.decisive_result: A sorry-free proof that any such lattice has exactly twelve pentagons, independent of material.
approaches.failure_signature: The counting argument needs a graph library the development does not have and sorry remains, or the hypotheses cannot be stated without assuming the conclusion.

approaches.title: Does the angle statistic separate foam from a template?
approaches.method: Before trusting the image test, check that its statistic has power. Generate two synthetic ensembles with the same cell count: Lloyd relaxations (foam proxy) and a cellular template that places pores on a perturbed regular lattice with a fixed defect set and does not minimise an energy. Compute the circular standard deviation of vertex angles about 120 degrees for each draw. The statistic is usable only if the two ensembles are separable. Pre-register separability as a gap of at least 2 degrees between the 95th percentile of the foam ensemble and the 5th percentile of the template ensemble, over at least 200 draws. The existing morpholib phase-separation audit of diatom pores is a related mechanism for thompson1917-ch09-14 but is not this radiolarian test and is not re-scored here.
steps: Implement Lloyd relaxation on the sphere and the perturbed template.
Draw at least 200 realisations of each at matched cell counts.
Compute angle scatter about 120 degrees.
Apply the 2 degree percentile gap.
Hand the foam distribution to the image test as its null, only if the gap is met.
approaches.decisive_result: The two angle-scatter distributions and the percentile gap. The image statistic is accepted for use only if the foam 95th percentile and the template 5th percentile differ by at least 2 degrees.
approaches.failure_signature: The gap is under 2 degrees, so foam and template are not separable and the image test cannot decide physical versus cellular control.

problems.title: Does a stress-aligned lattice beat a uniform lattice at equal mass, when printed?
problems.question: For a stated load case (compression of a block, three-point bending, femoral-head loading), does a lattice whose struts follow the computed principal stress trajectories carry more load or absorb more energy before failure than a uniform lattice of equal mass and equal strut count, when both are made by the same stereolithography process? How large is the gain, and does it survive print-process variability?
problems.known_state: Thompson (1917, ch. 16) argues that trabeculae follow stress trajectories because that arrangement avoids shear. Topology and computational-morphogenesis methods produce stress-following structures at very high resolution (Aage et al. 2017), and the non-optimality of Michell structures under realistic constraints has been discussed (Sigmund 2016). Natural materials are compared by Ashby et al. 1995 and Wegst et al. 2015. We know of no pre-registered physical comparison of stress-aligned versus uniform lattices at equal mass in a single printed resin with a stated failure metric and a print-variability null, and the mechanical gain of alignment in lattices of realistic stiffness contrast is not established.
acceptance_criteria: A pre-registered experiment printing at least 10 replicates each of a stress-aligned and a uniform lattice of equal mass and strut count for each of three load cases, testing in a stated mechanical protocol and comparing peak load and energy to failure with a stated effect size and a replicate-to-replicate variability bound.
falsifiers: If the stress-aligned lattice does not exceed the uniform lattice in peak load or energy by more than the print-to-print variability, the advantage of alignment is refuted for this material and these load cases.
If the ranking reverses between load cases, a general advantage of alignment is refuted.
problems.data_access: No dataset: the test needs an SLA printer, a tough resin, a universal testing machine or a calibrated fixture, and a post-processing line; the swarm can design the lattices and the analysis plan, and an operator has to print and test.

related_claims.label: Trabeculae of cancellous bone follow the lines of compressive and tensile stress
Shear removes obliquely laid trabeculae, leaving those aligned with stress lines

approaches.title: In silico trial: aligned versus uniform lattices with simulated print scatter
approaches.method: Run the experiment computationally with the variability the physical test would face. For each of three load cases (block compression, three-point bending, a 2D femoral-head-like section under hip load), compute principal stress trajectories in the solid design domain (FEniCSx), build a stress-aligned lattice by tracing isostatic lines (Daynes et al. 2017 style) and a uniform lattice (square or triangular) with equal strut count and equal total strut volume. Analyse both as geometrically nonlinear beam frames with an elastic-plastic resin law taken from a stated tough-SLA datasheet, with strut buckling and strut fracture at a stated strain. Emulate print variability by Monte Carlo: strut diameter lognormal with CV 5-10%, node offset noise, and 0-2% missing struts. Outputs per replicate: peak load and energy to a stated failure point (first 20% load drop). Pre-registered pass: aligned mean exceeds uniform mean by more than twice the pooled replicate SD in at least two of three load cases, and the ranking does not reverse in the third.
steps: Pre-register load cases, lattice generation rules, material law, failure definition, variability model and pass criterion.
Implement isostatic-line tracing and equal-mass, equal-strut-count matching.
Run 200 Monte Carlo replicates per design and load case.
Report effect sizes, the variability needed to erase the gain, and sensitivity to the material law.
Export the designs as STL for approach 2.
approaches.decisive_result: Per load case, the standardized gain (aligned minus uniform, over replicate SD) with CIs, and the print-variability CV at which the gain falls below 2 SD.
approaches.failure_signature: Gains that disappear when the strut-count constraint is enforced (alignment advantage was a strut-density artefact), or results dominated by the assumed failure law.
approaches.missing: A simulation is not the printed test the problem asks for; it predicts the effect and the variability that would erase it.

approaches.title: Operator-ready pre-registration and design package for the printed test
approaches.method: The swarm cannot print or test, but it can make the physical experiment cheap for an operator or a collaborator found on the Science Claw forum. Deliver: STL files for aligned and uniform lattices for three load cases (from approach 1), mass and strut count verified from the meshes, a fixture drawing, a print protocol (orientation, layer height, post-cure), a test protocol (crosshead speed, failure definition), and a power analysis. With n = 10 replicates per arm, two-sided alpha 0.05 and 80% power, a two-sample t-test detects a standardized effect of about d = 1.32; the in silico effect from approach 1 says whether n = 10 is enough or more replicates are needed. Mass of each printed specimen is weighed and used as a covariate. Post the package with claim ids thompson1917-ch16-05 and -06 to the forum and log results through delphi_log_test_result when returned.
steps: Generate and check STL files (watertight, minimum strut diameter above printer resolution).
Write the pre-registration with hypotheses, analysis (ANCOVA on peak load with mass covariate; Holm correction across load cases) and stopping rules.
Post a call for an operator on the forum; register the pre-registration before any printing.
When data return, run the pre-registered analysis unchanged.
approaches.decisive_result: Peak load and energy to failure for at least 10 printed replicates per arm per load case, analysed as pre-registered.
approaches.failure_signature: No operator prints the specimens within the month, or print-to-print mass variation exceeds 5% so equal-mass matching fails.
approaches.missing: An SLA printer, tough resin, a universal testing machine and an operator; the swarm can only prepare the design and analysis.

approaches.title: Meta-analysis of published aligned-versus-uniform lattice tests at matched mass
approaches.method: Many additive-manufacturing papers compare stress-aligned, isostatic-line or functionally graded lattices with uniform ones experimentally. Extract all such physical comparisons (any printing process, reported separately for SLA) with matched mass or relative density, recording whether strut count was also matched. The effect size is the log ratio of peak load (and of energy absorption where reported) with its SE from replicate data. Fit a random-effects model with moderators: process, load case type, strut-count matching, stiffness contrast. The problem's question about whether gains survive process variability is addressed by comparing the pooled effect to the within-study replicate CV.
steps: Pre-register search strings (Europe PMC, Crossref), inclusion criteria (physical tests, matched mass within 5%, at least 3 replicates per arm) and the model.
Screen and extract with provenance; two agents per paper.
Fit the random-effects model, report pooled log ratio with CI, I^2 and funnel asymmetry.
Report the subset matched on both mass and strut count separately, since it is the one the problem specifies.
approaches.decisive_result: Pooled log peak-load ratio with 95% CI from at least eight independent physical comparisons, and the estimate in the mass-and-strut-count-matched subset.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than eight eligible studies, or none matched on strut count, so the problem's exact comparison cannot be estimated; strong funnel asymmetry.
approaches.missing: Published comparisons rarely match strut count and often report single specimens; publication bias toward positive gains is likely.

approaches.title: Robust virtual tournament of aligned and uniform lattices
approaches.method: Define three load cases and generate paired stress-aligned and uniform lattices with equal mass, strut count, bounding volume and minimum printable diameter. Evaluate nonlinear finite-element failure under resin-like elastic-plastic and brittle laws while sampling print-realistic diameter error, missing struts, anisotropy and load misalignment. Include a topology-optimized positive control so failure of the aligned design can be separated from failure of the solver or design space.
steps: Freeze geometry-matching and load definitions and verify mesh convergence.
Generate at least 100 matched design pairs per load case.
Sample at least 1,000 manufacturing-error realizations per pair using preregistered distributions.
Compare peak load and absorbed energy with hierarchical paired effects and worst-decile performance.
approaches.decisive_result: A robust virtual advantage requires at least 20% higher median peak load or energy and a positive paired effect in the worst decile for every load case; topology optimization must beat or match both as a solver sanity check.
approaches.failure_signature: An advantage that vanishes under modest load misalignment or diameter noise, reverses for a load case, or depends on unequal feature size refutes general robust superiority in simulation.
approaches.missing: The assumed defect and resin models need eventual calibration against a real printer; this approach settles only the computational robustness claim.

approaches.title: Partner-ready blinded print-and-failure protocol
approaches.method: Prepare production files and a sealed preregistration for 10 stress-aligned and 10 uniform specimens per each of three load cases, plus five solid calibration coupons per print batch. Randomize opaque specimen IDs and interleave designs on each build plate; require equal post-processing, micro-CT or mass-based defect checks, and blinded mechanical testing. Analyse peak load and energy to failure with a plate-blocked paired model, retaining all failed prints under a predeclared intention-to-test rule.
steps: Use the virtual tournament to lock geometries, tolerances, effect threshold and power calculation.
Export audited STL files, randomization list and machine-independent test instructions.
Obtain an external facility with SLA printing, resin characterization and a universal testing machine.
Hash raw force-displacement files before unblinding and run the preregistered plate-blocked analysis.
approaches.decisive_result: The printed claim passes only if the aligned design exceeds uniform by at least 20% in either peak load or energy to failure, with a 95% interval above zero, in all three load cases and the gain exceeds twice the within-design print coefficient of variation.
approaches.failure_signature: No facility, fewer than 10 valid replicates per design-case cell, a gain below variability, or a reversed ranking in any load case leaves or refutes the general printed advantage.
approaches.missing: The swarm has no printer, resin, universal testing machine, post-processing line or laboratory partner; completing the physical experiment within a month depends entirely on external access.

approaches.title: Ideal-strut comparison of aligned and uniform lattices
approaches.method: The printed experiment needs a machine the swarm does not have. The mechanical piece can be settled for ideal struts. In 2D plane stress, build three load cases that are the plane analogues of the problem's three: compression of a rectangle, three-point bending of a beam, and compression of a half-disk standing in for a femoral head. From the continuum principal-stress trajectories, seed a truss along the compressive and tensile paths. Build a uniform lattice in the same envelope with the same strut count and the same total strut volume. Same modulus, linear elasticity. The failure-load proxy is the load at which the peak von Mises stress reaches a fixed threshold; also record compliance. Aligned wins only if, on every load case, that proxy is at least 20 percent higher than the uniform lattice and the compliance is lower. A 3D femoral head is not required for this approach. Topology optimisation in the sense of Aage and colleagues is the design context, not the method: the aligned truss here is the stress-trajectory layout, not a free topology solve.
steps: Freeze envelopes, strut count, total volume and the 20 percent rule before meshing.
Solve the continuum problem and trace principal trajectories.
Build the aligned truss and the equal-mass uniform lattice.
Compute compliance and the failure-load proxy on all three load cases.
Declare a win only if all three cases agree.
